data.title: I travelled the ‘border’ between North and South. Here’s what I learnt
data.description:
A sign by the estuary warns of danger, but it’s hard to see much to be afraid of here apart from the nettles and a fairly ominous sky. Under the Severn Bridge, on a spit of land on the river’s west side, it seems peaceful enough. Traffic roars overhead, but you can’t see the cars from below. There’s birdsong and the smell of wet foliage, glimmering water fringed by sodden sand and then cracked earth. It doesn’t feel like a border, but I’m standing at the far western end of England’s North-South divide.

There is, of course, no official line across England’s midriff. No razor-wire fences or passport checks mark where the South ends and the North begins. But nor is the boundary a figment of our imagination. We’ve heard enough jokes about the Watford Gap to know that Southerners see the North – the people, the places, the culture – as somehow different. And we Northerners, admittedly, can be bloody-minded about our Northern identity.

But how entrenched does the North-South divide remain today, after years of political talk of levelling up, Northern powerhouses and ill-fated high-speed rail connections? How much does our geography still shape how we see those from elsewhere in the country? And where, actually, does the notional dividing line start and end?

Apparently, not where you might expect. Recent YouGov data from almost 46,000 adults in England revealed that many people along the borders of the areas classified as North, South and Midlands don’t place themselves in the same regions government maps would suggest. Feelings of “Northernness” extended south of the regional borders, the pollsters found, while in the parts of East Anglia that supposedly sit in the South, people don’t all feel Southern. In short, like many types of identity, it’s complicated.

With that in mind, I have set out to travel along an unofficial boundary line between the North and South of England – one commonly used in academic research – to interrogate these feelings and explore what the divide means today. My editor has suggested I walk the entire 340 miles from Beachley Point on the Severn estuary to the Wash, between Lincolnshire and Norfolk, possibly in one go. I have counter-suggested the use of a motor vehicle.

The journey is a personal one. Having grown up in Leeds, my Northern identity is one I have insisted on throughout my adult life (which I’ve spent mostly in the South). When I started writing my debut crime thriller novel, The House on Otley Road, I knew it had to be set in West Yorkshire. Home.

The tug of the North has never left me, and I spend much of my time on the East Coast Main Line, travelling to and from where I spent my youth. But I’m surprised to find that it supposedly begins more or less where I’m standing by the Severn. The first (and only) person I encounter on the footpath here is Justin Charnock, 37. He identifies as Southern (this is fair – he comes from near Bristol) and thinks “people in the North are a lot nicer than people in the South” (also fair). “More welcoming,” he says.

It’s a commonly held perception, mentioned frequently by those I meet on my journey – almost all of whom have strong ideas about how Northerners differ from Southerners.

Charnock thinks being Southern traditionally means being “wealthier; a lot more aloof; snobby; much less hospitable, welcoming, friendly or helpful”. Working in the South West (he won’t divulge his job), he never gets tipped and “often people are a bit snooty”.

‘It’s become very middle class here’

Behind the popular images of Northerners lie some dispiriting numbers. The North East remains the region with the lowest healthy life expectancy at birth (HLE), at 57 years, according to the most recent figures from the Office for National Statistics (ONS). It has had the lowest HLE in every period since the ONS began measuring it. The South East remains the region with the highest HLE (63 years for men, 64.3 years for women).

A similar disparity can be seen in economic activity. In 2023, London had the highest gross domestic product per capita, at £69,077, while the North East had the lowest, at £28,583. It is worth noting, though, that the poverty rate is higher in London (26 per cent) than anywhere else in the country, according to figures from the charity Joseph Rowntree Foundation.

Meanwhile, perceptions of Northerners and Southerners that seem to stem from our economic histories – the North as industrial, the South as the country’s financial engine – have stubbornly persisted.

The first stop on my journey is Brockweir, a scenic Gloucestershire village on the river Wye. Old stone houses are painted in creamy yellow, pale blue and white, while green hills rise behind them. All the villagers seem to know each other. They all have dogs, and their dogs know each other too. The community owns its pub, the 16th-century Brockweir Inn.

“We tried to sell our bodies [to raise the money for it], but we’re all too old,” says Carol Knight, 76. (I think she’s joking.)

Her family has lived here for centuries. “It’s become very middle class,” says the suntanned, denim-dungaree-clad former English teacher, while clutching a bunch of Whitsuntide boss flowers and the leads of her two labradors. “Property prices have skyrocketed.”

Does this mean Brockweir must be Southern? House prices are, after all, a stark divider between North and South. Prices may be rising more steeply in the North at present, but the gap remains vast, even after removing London from the equation: in March 2026, the average house price across the South East and South West was £340,000, compared with £188,500 across the North East and North West.

‘We need more Northern leaders’

I travel onwards, trying to keep close to the Wye, down winding lanes bordered by verdant hedgerows and cow parsley. I stop at Upper Redbrook, where I can’t find a pub, or a shop, or a human, then Staunton, where the 18th-century pub isn’t open yet (it’s still too early). Traffic rattles through the village of silent modern houses.

In the Herefordshire village of Lea, I encounter a friendly pair of Scousers who decamped here long ago. Mike Tyson, a 46-year-old roofer and carpenter (“Yes, it’s my real name,” he says, for probably the millionth time), talks of his daughter’s “Northern attitude”.

What is it? “Friendlier, more easy-come, easy-go. ‘Chippy’ is the right phrase.”

The men are not the only ones to claim Northerners have a different (better?) sense of humour. But there’s uncertainty about whether we’re in the North or the South here – the consensus seems to be the middle – but Tyson believes there’s more money to be made down here than up in Liverpool.

Tied up with the question of economic activity and affluence is that of political power. Devolution to England’s cities and regions has given some control to communities far from Westminster. Whether it has helped those communities feel less overlooked is uncertain. Phil Henesey, 71, who is drinking in a beer garden with Tyson in the late-afternoon sunshine, says the North still feels farther (figuratively) from Westminster decision making.

“That’s why we need more Northern leaders,” he says.

He is speaking not long before the enthroning of a Northern leader in Downing Street. Andy Burnham, the Liverpool-born former Mayor of Greater Manchester, has made much of his links to, and concern for, the North of England. The new PM has created a No 10 North. In doing so, he has set himself up to be judged on how successfully he makes Northerners feel more connected to the centre of power. Also on how he does this without alienating the South.

‘There’s more chivalry in the North’

It’s raining when I reach Ledbury, the sky a grey-white sheet. The Tudor buildings are picture-perfect and well preserved. “It’s very much Middle England,” says a shopkeeper on the high street who doesn’t want to be named. “Did you ever see Keeping up Appearances? It’s full of Hyacinth Buckets [here].”

He identifies as a Southerner. “When you go up North, it’s dark,” he says. “It’s a funny old thing, that divide.”

Declan Butler, a 68-year-old Irishman who moved to Britain in the 1970s and now runs a gift shop down the road, thinks Ledbury is “probably more Southern”, judging by its disposable income.

“I had a couple in here from North Yorkshire at the weekend and they spoke to me as if we were old friends, whereas people from the South East are much more reserved,” he says. “If I was to choose a Southerner or a Northerner to be friends with, I’d choose a Northerner, because they’re friendlier. They’re probably harder workers. They’re grafters.”

He concedes that Cockneys and people from Essex can be friendly, too. Has he been to the North much? “I’ve been to Birmingham,” he offers.

Crossing into Worcestershire, I see the grey-blue shadow of the hills rise up ahead. I pass an old roadside chapel and an abandoned filling station, and arrive at Bredon, where the local Spar sells cider on tap.

“I thought the North started at Crewe,” muses Steve Fowler, an ex-Army man, inside the still-quiet Royal Oak pub, where there’s horse racing on the TV. He’s surprised to hear that by some definitions he is in the North right now. A Southerner by birth (Surrey), he awards the North another point for humour. “The funniest comedians are Northerners,” he says.

“I think [people] are more materialistic in the South,” says David Gray, a semi-retired gardener from Scotland. “There’s a lot more chivalry in the North.”

“It’s all about survival in the North,” chips in Paul Sefton, a retired butcher. He came here from North Wales 30 years ago “purely because someone said to me my kids would never get a proper job up North”.

‘The Cotswolds is becoming the Home Counties’

The North-South divide has been with us for a long time, chronicled and perpetuated by our art and culture. Elizabeth Gaskell’s North and South (published 1855) contrasts England’s tranquil, idyllic South with a grimy industrial North plagued by poverty and suffering. Almost 150 years later, David Peace evoked a dark and lawless North in his fictional Red Riding quartet. There was always something harder and edgier about the most famous Northern bands than their Southern counterparts. Contrast the Beatles with the Kinks, Oasis with Blur.

Yet in today’s hyperconnected society, how long can such differences last?

“It’s flattened out quite a bit by sheer mobility,” says Steve Fowler. And, he says, by exposure to the internet. “You would have to go very deep into the countryside, to very isolated communities, to find residual differences.”

In the Plough Inn in Stretton-on-Fosse, Warwickshire, Gordon Everett, 59, says, with both sadness and pride, “This is one of the last old-fashioned drinking pubs.” Local accents are waning a lot, he says, touching on the most overt marker of Northern or Southern identity. When he was a boy, you could tell the difference in accents between people from two local villages that lay just three miles apart. “Now, everyone’s got this flat English accent.”

Non-locals, he says, have come to the area and changed it. “The Cotswolds is becoming the Home Counties.”

Still, tracing this line across the country is a lesson in the extent to which our villages and small towns either cling to their past or else are haunted by it. Between Bredon and Stretton-on-Fosse, I pass houses with names such as the Old Bakehouse, the Old Stoves. A croquet club and a country clothing store. Less picturesque: a dead badger on the A44.

In Brackley, Northamptonshire, there’s a similar nostalgia in evidence. On the high street, there’s the Old Bakery and the Old Hall Bookshop. The sign for Brackley Community Shops is painted in old-fashioned fairground colours. One of these shops offers tattoos, but still.

In the Courtyard Shops farther along, I’m reminded of one of those mock-Victorian streets you find in museums, except there’s a vape shop here. Browsers are welcome, says a sticker in the window, and they’re also on CCTV.

A 75-year-old woman I meet in the town, when I ask what Northerners are like, suggests they’re either industrious farmers or else they work in “industrial places”. I don’t have the heart to tell her that no one I know in West Yorkshire does any such thing.

Did you know Brackley is in fact north of the North-South divide, I ask Anne Mellor, a volunteer in a local charity shop? “No,” she says, “we thought we were in the middle, surrounded by HS2.”

Depending on where you are in the North, transport links can be a sore point – and another marker of difference from the South. Burnham might be proud of his re-regulated Bee Network buses in Manchester, but raise the subject of the still-non-existent tram service in Leeds and that fabled Northern grit might give way to heavy sighs of Northern frustration.

In the North East, poor transport links were said last year to put more than 30 per cent of the region at risk of poverty. In 2022, lack of transport connectivity was found by the Centre for Cities to cost the North £16bn a year in productivity losses. Against this backdrop, HS2 has become a punchline, not an answer.

‘They’re parochial and territorial’

I’m travelling to Silverstone, Northamptonshire, which is famous for a different sort of transport. Pictures of motor-racing heroes adorn the walls of the village pub, the White Horse. I pass through a familiar landscape of roundabouts and roadworks before arriving. A poster on the village noticeboard invites me to become the best version of myself. (I decline.)

Gary Baird, 38, who runs the pub, thinks the North is more working class, while the South attracts more tourism. No one, he argues, goes to Hull on holiday.

Onwards to Rushden, Northants, a “historic boot and shoe town”, passing en route an American diner, a Starbucks, a Travelodge, a McDonald’s, a Toby Carvery and a new-build housing estate. I could be anywhere now. I don’t know whether I’m North or South, my senses are scrambled, or numbed by the dreary uniformity of our in-between spaces.

But in Rushden, for the first time, I feel I could be in the North. Behind the bar in the town’s Working Men’s Club, 30-year-old Tomethia Bartley confirms, “They’re Northerners here.” (She’s not – she’s from London.) “They’re all in a community together. Everyone knows everyone.”

She’s wearing a T-shirt saying, “Don’t like me? F--- off. Problem solved.” I don’t know how Northern or Southern this sentiment is.

Howard, 67, a former helicopter pilot enjoying a pint in the club with his partner, Lynette Keirnan, says: “I was married to a woman from Lancashire. She was bloody weird, actually. They seem to see things differently up there. They’re very parochial and territorial.

“They eat food like barm cakes [a bread roll from the North West] and black peas,” he adds. “They feel disenfranchised, I think.”

But out on the high street, it doesn’t feel so different here from many post-industrial towns further North, with grand old Victorian buildings and the sense of better days being behind it. There’s a kebab shop and an amusement arcade now. A nail bar, a Poundstretcher and, curiously, a large reptile specialist called House of Venom.

Deeply ingrained perceptions

The land flattens out as I enter Lincolnshire, stopping briefly in Market Deeping for a scalding portion of battered fish. “Sunny days are here at last,” it says on a small blackboard inside the Market Gate Deli. Outside, a fine rain falls. An unseasonable chill hangs in the early June air.

My odyssey ends in Norfolk, where I meet arable farmer Richard Ward, 55. “Where am I?” I ask.

“You’re probably North more than anything, because that’s the North Sea,” he says, pointing to the horizon, where I can’t see anything but farmland. A few years ago, a bomb squad came to remove a load of Second World War ordnance found in the fields. “It was quite a hairy experience,” says Ward.

Do people fish out there? I ask, pointing vaguely to where the sea should be. No, he says. “It’s dead vegetation and horrible black, boggy clay soil.”

I finish my journey not far from this, by a soggy field overlooking some marshland. The sun has finally emerged. Some desultory wasps buzz above the glistening wet grass. A crow caws, a cockerel crows and my feet are becoming very wet.

The conversations I’ve had along my journey have shown that, despite our increasingly homogenised culture, perceptions of differences between Northerners and Southerners remain deeply ingrained. Perhaps we will always retain these in some form.

As Richard Collett writes in his book Along the Borders, “We carve landscapes apart to define our very sense of self and identity.”

I recognise this impulse. And I’m not going to claim it’s all grim down South, but I’ll always be Northern and proud.

The House on Otley Road by Rosa Silverman (£16.99, HQ/HarperCollins) is out now.

data.title: Just 270 shoplifters behind almost 30,000 offences
data.description:
Just 270 suspected prolific shoplifters accounted for nearly 30,000 offences.

The thieves averaged 105 shoplifting offences each – and these were just the crimes formally reported to the police in which officers had identified a suspect. They do not include other thefts for which they may not have been caught.

One of the most prolific shoplifters was identified in Sussex as being linked to 247 offences in six years – equivalent to a crime being reported every 10 days.

The data, obtained under freedom of information laws by the BBC, showed that overall, the 270 were linked to 28,415 shoplifting offences in England and Wales between 2020-21 and 2025-26.

It was based on figures from 27 of the 43 forces asked to provide data on the 10 suspects they had linked to shoplifting offences.

One shoplifter, Jeff Ashman, estimated that he walked out of shops with goods worth £400 to £500 daily.

“It’s mind-boggling,” he said, describing how much he had stolen from stores in Hastings to fuel his addictions to heroin and crack cocaine. “I know the misery and grief and despair that I have caused these people for a long period of time.”

He said he had put shoplifting firmly behind him – but prolific offenders continue to plague communities across England.

The number of shoplifting offences remains at close to record levels of 500,000 in the past year. It is estimated that 10 per cent of shoplifters are responsible for 68 per cent of all thefts.

Retail chiefs say thieves have become “more brazen, more organised and more aggressive” following a four-fold increase in shoplifting since the Covid pandemic.

Repeat offenders are estimated to be four times more likely to be violent or use a weapon than other shoplifters, according to research by Auror, a retail crime intelligence agency that helps to identify and target prolific thieves.

Police forces are increasingly deploying their officers against prolific offenders, based on the fact that prosecuting them will have the biggest effect in reducing the scale of the thefts.

Sarah Jones, the policing minister, said shoplifting was a “pernicious crime that, for too long, has gone unpunished”.

She added: “They need to know that they are going to be punished for what they have done.”

Although police have started to reduce the number of shoplifting crimes and are bringing more offenders to justice, they are frustrated that courts are too slow to convict and sentence them.

Matt Twist, the Metropolitan Police’s assistant commissioner, requested that ministers implement “fast-track” justice for prolific shoplifters so that they can be sentenced within days of a charge.

He also called for stricter punishments by increasing the use of criminal behaviour orders to lock up more offenders if they continued to offend.

“I know why retailers and the public are concerned about a sense of lawlessness. I know why they’re concerned about a sense that people can commit these crimes with impunity,” Mr Twist told The Telegraph.

“We are absolutely determined to bear down on this and to deal with the repeat offenders, those that cause retail staff the most concern, those that put people in fear.”

data.title: Healey must cut spending to rescue economy, warns Next boss
data.description:
The boss of Next has urged John Healey to get a grip of public spending in the Budget or risk condemning Britain’s economy to low growth and soaring debts.

Lord Wolfson, who is the longest-serving FTSE 100 company chief executive, said he expected a “slow, steady decline” in customer spending later this year as inflation gathers pace, mortgage rates rise and the jobs market weakens.

The high street chief said the prospects for growth for the British economy had become “more anaemic” over the past year and were “likely to get worse rather than better”.

He insisted that the only route out of the “predicament” facing the country was a combination of lower public spending and supply-side reforms, such as ripping up the planning system.

Lord Wolfson’s comments came as Next, which employs more than 20,000 people in the UK, revealed pre-tax profits rose 10.5pc to hit £569m in the six months to July. Overall sales rose 9pc to reach £3.5bn.

However, the Tory peer refused to join other business leaders in demanding major tax cuts, claiming it was “not a realistic approach” when the deficit is running at £100bn a year

He said: “I think that asking for tax cuts at this point in the cycle is futile.

“But asking for them not to go up more, asking for government to live within its means, asking for measures that can boost the economy without spending money, I think, is a more realistic approach.”

He added: “Any organisation cannot carry on spending significantly more than his income, and in one way or another, that problem has to be addressed.”

Lord Wolfson also called for immediate major reform of the planning system to kick start growth.

He said: “The biggest single factor holding the UK coming back is the planning laws, building regulations, and all of the various environmental, archaeological, biodiversity rules around building, which are holding us back.

“Releasing that pent-up demand would do a lot to boost growth.”

He went on to warn the Chancellor that further tax rises would only make the situation worse by stifling the growth that could deliver higher revenues for the Treasury.

Mr Healey will present his first Budget on Oct 28 against a backdrop of deteriorating public finances, rising inflation and higher borrowing costs.

Lord Wolfson, who has run Next for 25 years, turning it into one of Britain’s most profitable retailers, was particularly scathing about any plans for further taxes on investment.

He said profits distributed to shareholders as dividends are already being taxed at an effective rate of almost 52pc.

That is corporation tax of 25pc on the profits themselves and 36.75pc on the dividends paid out of those profits.

He added: “It might be tempting to think that higher taxes on investment affect only a small number of investors. They do not. Lower investment means less growth, and that affects everyone.

“Next was one of many to warn that increasing taxes and regulation on jobs would undermine employment. Unfortunately that concern now appears well-founded.

“Our concern today is that increasing tax on investment will reduce investment in the UK, and that will be bad for employment and bad for growth.”

Lord Wolfson made his comments as he unveiled a “much better than expected” set of first-half financial results boosted by the long, hot summer.

Profit guidance for the full year has been raised to £1.26bn.

data.title: Kremlin seizes Nestlé’s Russian assets in new crackdown
data.description:
Nestlé said it is assessing its options after Vladimir Putin ordered the seizure of its Russian business.

The KitKat maker suggested it would take action to protect its rights after the Kremlin announced a presidential decree taking control of the Swiss company’s assets on Thursday.

It told shareholders: “The company is assessing the situation and its options.

“Nestlé is committed to taking all necessary steps to protect its rights and ensure continuity of business operations in the interests of all stakeholders, particularly its employees.”

Russia has tightened control over foreign-owned assets since the start of the Ukraine war in 2022.

A 2023 decree signed by Putin gives Moscow the power to place ‌assets from countries it deems “unfriendly” ‌under temporary administration.

The mechanism has been used to take control ​of the Russian subsidiaries of Danone and Carlsberg.

Nestlé shares fell 1.7pc on Friday in the wake of the Kremlin’s order, which also put the Russian business of French ​supermarket group ‌Auchan into a temporary administration.

The decree also covers the Russian subsidiaries of French logistics group FM Logistic and the former Leroy Merlin DIY chain, now known as Lemana Pro.

Each company’s assets have been transferred to a company called LEV Management.

Nestlé has six factories in Russia producing coffee, pet care and infant formula.

⁠It generated sales of about 2bn Swiss francs (£1.8bn) in Russia in 2021, the last year it released figures, and has about 7,000 employees there.

Warren Ackerman, an analyst at Barclays, said the Kremlin’s order means the “risk of Nestlé losing the business looks materially higher”.

However, Jean-Philippe Bertschy of the Swiss investment bank Vontobel said he expected the financial impact to Nestlé would be small “given Russia’s limited contribution to group sales”.

He said Russia now accounted for just over 1pc of the group’s sales, down from around 2pc before the Ukraine war.

It has suspended “the vast majority of sales, non-essential imports, advertising and capital investment”, he said, while continuing to supply essential food items.

Moscow took control of French dairy company Danone’s Russian business ‌and beer company Carlsberg’s stake in a local brewer in 2023.

Danone ​was removed from the list of assets under temporary Russian state ​management in March 2024 amid reports that a Russian businessman ⁠known for his pro-war ⁠credentials planned to buy the business at a steep discount.

In December 2024, Carlsberg sold its shares in Baltika Breweries in a management buyout.

Jon Cox, a Kepler Cheuvreux analyst, said such experiences did not bode well for Nestlé.

He said: “Ultimately, Nestlé may end up losing those assets – around 2pc of its sales and cash tied up in Russia – for the foreseeable future and any compensation is unlikely to be ​an offset.”

data.title: Even The Canary doesn’t deserve to be debanked
data.description:
Is another wave of debanking underway?

The Leftist news site The Canary reports that it has had two bank accounts frozen and that it now has no choice but to suspend its operation altogether. Many will be delighted that The Canary has stopped publishing – but you don’t have to support the platform to worry about the power that banks now exercise over our free speech and free press. The Canary’s shutdown should be a wake-up call to us all.

The Canary claims it was given no forewarning, no explanation and no opportunity to challenge the initial decision by Lloyds to freeze its account in June, just two weeks after it expanded into printing editions for newsagents. Now, the outlet reports that Metro Bank has frozen another account associated with the company, leaving them unable to operate.

Coutts’ debanking of Nigel Farage in 2023 was perhaps the most high-profile example of political debanking but it’s far from the only one. Before Farage’s account closure, in 2020 Barclays closed two accounts associated with a Christian charity Core Issues Trust after it was the target of a LGBT social-media campaign against conversion therapy. Muslim organisations have long reported debanking issues, with waves of account closures over years.

The investigation that followed the Farage debanking scandal showed his was not an isolated case. It examined 84 other accounts of “politically exposed” people that had been closed by NatWest around the same time – a 10 per cent sample of relevant closures. NatWest, which owns Coutts, initially claimed that Farage’s sudden account closure had nothing to do with the Reform leader’s political views. However, documents showed senior staff had internally complained about his “xenophobic, chauvinistic and racist views” and deemed them to be “at odds with our position” before his account was closed.

Corporations are entitled to their relentless, insufferable position-taking, flag-waving and ethics-washing and they are entitled to choose or lose customers as they like – but under the Equality Act 2010, they cannot discriminate against people for their race, religion, sexuality or indeed most political views. Fair and equal treatment is a very fundamental principle in English law – and we ought to be equally alarmed by political debanking whoever it might target.

I couldn’t find any records of The Canary writing about, let alone raising the alarm about, Farage’s debanking. The Left and Right silos of concern about our country’s mounting censorship problem are part of the reason it has been able to reach such a crisis point. And now, Canary staff members arguably find themselves in an even worse position than Farage. The Canary’s direct debits have bounced, temporarily taking its website offline; projects have been cancelled, invoices can’t be settled, and staff can’t be paid.

Censorship by debanking has not just a financial cost, nor just a democratic cost, but a significant human cost too. That’s why it’s so powerful. Few people are so determined to express their most unpopular opinions that they will risk their livelihoods to do it.

George Galloway claimed this week that he can’t pay his mortgage, can’t pay his tax bill and can’t care for his 92-year-old mother as he too has just been debanked. The Workers Party of Britain leader says he was a customer of the Bank of Scotland – part of the Lloyds Banking Group – for 39 years before his account was closed without forewarning or explanation.

Banks insist account closures are never politically driven, but people and organisations sharing remarkably similar politics seem to have their accounts frozen around the same time.

The banks might have entirely legitimate reasons for closing The Canary and Galloway’s bank accounts. But their refusal to tell their customers why accounts have been shut down doesn’t suggest so. It is understandable, for privacy reasons, that the banks don’t talk about these cases to the public, but if they’d had the decency to talk to the account owners before their financial executions, they could at least reassure the public that they had provided their reasoning privately.

Instead, the banks’ silence speaks volumes. It shows their total indifference to the damage they are inflicting on our freedom of speech and freedom of the press.

In the absence of any explanation, The Canary and Galloway are prompted to speculate about why they have been targeted. Is it a conspiracy against their pro-Palestine views? Is it the national security apparatus manoeuvring against them? Are they such a threat to the establishment?

The answer seems to be that banks associate politics with risk and are constantly seeking to “de-risk”. But we need to stop treating controversial opinions as a risk. They are a feature, not a flaw, of a living, breathing democracy.

data.title: Family TV time is dead ... and doomscrolling killed it
data.description:
The days of families gathering around the TV could soon be at an end, with young Britons increasingly glued to their own screens.

Almost half of the time (44pc) UK adults spend watching, reading or listening to commercial media is now spent alone, according to new figures from advertising trade body the Institute of Practitioners in Advertising (IPA).

That figure is 10 percentage points higher than in 2015. It means adults now spend just over two and a half hours consuming media on their own each day.

Solo viewing is most common among 16 to 34-year-olds, who spend 46pc of their media time in isolation, up by more than a fifth from a decade ago. That equates to two hours and 45 minutes per day.

Across all age groups, solo viewing time is considerably higher for men than women.

The shift in viewing habits comes amid an explosion of choice for British consumers, who can now take their pick from a plethora of streaming and on-demand options rather than a narrow choice of TV channels and radio stations.

It has led to a fragmentation in the way media is consumed, with younger audiences particularly isolated. It has also resulted in a drop in the number of shared cultural moments.

Among all UK adults, smartphones now account for the same share of commercial media time as TV sets – 34pc.

However, smartphones represent 49pc of viewing time among 16 to 34-year-olds. This comes despite growing concerns over habits such as “doomscrolling”. The TV viewing among younger audiences has fallen from 32pc in 2015 to 21pc in 2026.

Just under half the time young people spend viewing commercial media is on apps such as TikTok, Instagram or YouTube.

Meanwhile, the time adults spend talking face-to-face per day is down by 4pc from 2015 to seven hours and 25 minutes. For 16 to 34-year-olds, it is down 11pc to seven hours and 10 minutes.

Simon Frazier, of the IPA, said: “Consider a Saturday night in a family home in the late 1980s and everyone would possibly be glued to Beadle’s About, sharing anecdotes and bonding over a shared experience.

“Compare that to today, when the likelihood is that the family will be on multiple screens in different rooms of the house. The shared media experience is increasingly under pressure.”

The figures highlight the challenge facing traditional broadcasters as viewers defect to online entertainment.

Commercial broadcasters such as ITV and Channel 4 are grappling with falling advertising revenues, while the BBC, which is funded by the licence fee and therefore not included in the IPA’s data, was overtaken by YouTube in audience numbers for the first time this year.

Despite the shift to solo viewing, streaming giants such as Netflix have been experimenting with traditional TV formats such as live events and weekly schedules in an effort to create shared moments to boost their fledgling advertising efforts.

Farhann Cachra, of Global, the media group behind radio stations LBC and Classic FM, said: “Personalisation risks becoming isolation, and with it an atomised society and a propensity to feed an individualised culture.

“At the same time, the human need for collective experience hasn’t shrunk, it’s just been squeezed into fewer moments. That scarcity is precisely what makes them so valuable.”

data.title: AI threatens £700bn exodus from Britain’s biggest banks
data.description:
British banks’ profits are at risk from AI bots moving customers’ cash out of zero-interest current accounts in search of better returns.

Savers could shift up to £700bn out of accounts that offer little or no returns and into savings products on the advice of AI chatbots, according to consultants at McKinsey.

Bank profits have soared in recent years as they benefit from the hundreds of billions of pounds held in customers’ current accounts by lending money out at a higher rate.

The gap between what banks pay their customers – which in the case of most current accounts is nothing – and what they earn on the loans they provide is called “net interest margin”. It is the single biggest source of bank profits.

However, McKinsey warned that those revenues could be under threat as powerful AI bots help consumers move their savings to services that offer better returns.

UK adults are among the worst at investing their household wealth out of the world’s major economies. An estimated seven million UK adults hold £10,000 or more of investible assets entirely in cash.

AI could change this, McKinsey said, because bots can quickly compare savings rates or even automatically move idle balances into higher-yield accounts.

If just 5pc to 10pc of bank balances are moved this way, the profits lenders make on deposits could drop by a fifth or more.

The “big four” high-street lenders made combined profits of £29.2bn in the first six months of this year, up 21pc on 2025 and John Healey, the Chancellor, has been considering a windfall tax on bank profits in his first Budget next month.

More than half of consumers in the UK already use AI tools and a quarter use the technology for financial tasks at least once a month. That figure rises to 59pc among high-income consumers.

British banks are increasingly competing with ChatGPT and Gemini for everyday financial advice. More people who use banking AI services turn to the technology industry’s chatbots than their bank’s in-house chatbot, McKinsey said.

Meanwhile, challenger banks such as Monzo and Revolut are increasingly eating into the business of mainstream banks and have been adding AI features to their own apps.

These smaller businesses have added tens of millions of customers with far smaller teams than traditional lenders.

McKinsey said that while customers might still have their salaries paid into their high-street accounts, they were using fintechs for day-to-day spending.

Revolut nearly tripled its number of customers between 2022 and 2025, while reducing its cost per customer by £3 during the same period.

data.title: GSK plots £400m Cambridge research hub in push for cancer breakthrough
data.description:
GlaxoSmithKline (GSK) will invest £400m in a major new science hub in Cambridge as part of plans to pour more money into developing new cancer drugs.

The pharmaceuticals giant said it planned to acquire a new 300,000 sq ft site on the Cambridge Biomedical Campus, which will house most of its research and development (R&D).

The new centre of excellence will employ more than 1,000 scientists, GSK said, with its researchers developing new vaccines, HIV treatments and cancer drugs.

However, the move will also end the FTSE 100 company’s 50-year relationship with Stevenage, Hertfordshire, which was previously its main UK research base. Some Stevenage staff will be asked to relocate to another lab in nearby Ware.

The investment in Cambridge comes as GSK seeks to ramp up its pipeline of medicines under Luke Miels, its new chief executive, who took on the role from Dame Emma Walmsley at the start of the year.

The company has been accelerating investment in cancer drugs after it acquired US-based Nuvalent in June for nearly £8bn.

GSK won approval from US medical regulators last week for Jideytro, a lung cancer treatment secured as part of the takeover of Nuvalent.

The decision to open a new Cambridge campus will bolster the Government’s efforts to turn the 100-mile corridor between Oxford and Cambridge into an economic powerhouse.

GSK said the investment would build its presence “in the heart of the UK’s life sciences ‘Golden Triangle’” – made up of Oxford, Cambridge and London.

Earlier this year, Rachel Reeves, the former chancellor, set out Labour’s ambition to turn the area into a hub for science businesses, building new homes and transport links to create Europe’s “Silicon Valley”.

The Cambridge Biomedical Campus already employs more than 22,000 people and hosts treatments for one million patients each year. GSK hopes to build its links with research hospitals in Cambridge and benefit from proximity to the University of Cambridge.

Mr Miels said: “This investment will accelerate our R&D and help us deliver new, competitive products.”

On Tuesday, GSK also announced plans for a major cost-cutting drive aimed at saving £1.9bn by 2029 to fund the development of new drugs. The savings are expected to include job cuts around the world, including reducing some back-office roles.

Alongside the plans for a new Cambridge site, GSK said it had launched 20 phase three trials as part of its plans to expand its pipeline of treatments.

These trials are the final stage of clinical testing before a drug is submitted to the Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency for approval.

Andy Burnham, the Prime Minister, said the £400m investment was “a vote of confidence in British business”.

Life science is one of eight sectors that form part of the Government’s modern industrial strategy.

The investment from GSK comes after its rival AstraZeneca announced that it would pour £200m into its Cambridge site, along with £100m for a project in Macclesfield, Cheshire.

GSK’s relocation to the Cambridge Biomedical Campus means Britain’s two largest pharmaceutical companies will neighbour each other in the city. GSK said it would keep its global headquarters in London.

data.title: AstraZeneca dumped by investors over £300bn US merger talks
data.description:
AstraZeneca shares have taken an £18bn hit after investors baulked at reports it was plotting a mega-merger with a US rival.

Shares in Britain’s second-most valuable company slumped on Monday after it emerged that AstraZeneca had held talks about a potential $400bn (£300bn) tie-up with Bristol Myers Squibb.

If completed, the merger would create one of the world’s largest pharmaceutical businesses. The potential deal would also raise fears that AstraZeneca could shift its business to the US in a blow to Britain.

However, analysts said it was a high-risk deal that risked destroying more value than it created. It would be one of the biggest mergers of all time, meaning any missteps could prove hugely costly, and would be likely to draw the attention of competition regulators and politicians.

News of the talks, first reported by the Financial Times, sent AstraZeneca’s shares plunging 9pc on Monday to their lowest level since September 2025.

Markus Manns, a portfolio manager at Union Investment and an ‌AstraZeneca ⁠shareholder, told Reuters: “A combination with Bristol ​does not make strategic or financial sense.

“Many past mega-mergers have destroyed value and there is no apparent need for Astra to do it.”

Jefferies analysts said in a note: “If there is ​one company that doesn’t need financial engineering, it’s AstraZeneca.”

Michael Leuchten, an analyst at Jefferies, said he was “perplexed” by the potential takeover. He said investors backed the company because of its consistent sales growth, not because management “go out and do big deals”.

AstraZeneca is worth around £184bn on the London Stock Exchange, while New York-listed Bristol Myers Squibb has a market value of $133bn.

Bristol Myers Squibb shares surged as much as 3.8pc on Wall Street on Monday.

Analysts said competition concerns would be the biggest hurdle to a deal as both companies have large cancer treatment businesses.

The potential deal could also trigger a political backlash from Donald Trump’s administration, Jefferies warned.

Mr Leuchten added: “AstraZeneca would effectively be a UK-based acquirer of one of America’s large Pharmas, at a time when US policymakers are focused on domestic manufacturing and strategic industries.”

The deal would raise questions about AstraZeneca’s continued links to Britain as Sir Pascal Soriot, its chief executive, pushes ahead with a pivot towards the US.

AstraZeneca upgraded its listing on the New York Stock Exchange last September to let American investors buy its shares directly, while keeping its listing in London.

The move put AstraZeneca’s New York listing on a par with that of London, in what was seen as a blow to the UK’s struggling stock market.

AstraZeneca subsequently struck a $50bn deal with the Trump administration to invest in US manufacturing and transatlantic research facilities.

At the time, Sir Pascal described the drugmaker as a “very American company”.

The business subsequently agreed to sell some medicines at a discount to the US Medicaid programme to avoid being hit with tariffs.

Despite this, Britain’s biggest drugmaker has insisted that it intends to remain headquartered in Cambridge and retain its listing on the London Stock Exchange.

Mr Leuchten said buying Bristol Myers Squibb as a way to shift permanently to the US would be “a fairly drastic way to go about it”.

However, Neil Birrell, the chief investment officer at Premier Miton, an AstraZeneca shareholder, said the likelihood of the pharmaceutical business shifting its shares to the US would increase if the Bristol Myers Squibb deal went ahead.

Mr Birrell added: “There hasn’t been a huge amount that I’ve seen coming out from any of the authorities – whether it be the Government or the London Stock Exchange – of any great substance to try and keep these sort of companies here.”

The Prime Minister said the talks were “a private matter for the companies involved”.

A No 10 spokesman said: “More broadly, the UK life sciences sector is one of our greatest national assets, driving innovation, skilled employment and investment across the country while developing medicines that improve health outcomes and save lives.”

AstraZeneca has around 10,000 staff at five UK sites, including 4,000 at its main facilities in Cambridge and Macclesfield and another 2,000 in London and Luton.

Steve Boden, a regional organiser at GMB Union, said he was seeking urgent assurances from AstraZeneca that jobs would be protected.

“These reports of a merger are causing great concern amongst AstraZeneca’s loyal workers. While no deal has been formally announced, mergers can create pressure to cut costs, so staff are understandably worrying about what this could mean for them.”

The proposed mega-merger will evoke memories of Pfizer’s attempts to take over AstraZeneca a decade ago.

The US company’s acquisition ultimately collapsed after a wave of resistance from the board and politicians alike.

Ed Miliband, then Labour leader, said at the time that Pfizer’s assurances about protecting research and saving jobs were “worthless”.

Bristol Myers Squibb is headquartered in Princeton, New Jersey, and was started in 1858, making it one of the US’s oldest pharmaceutical companies.

data.title: Octopus adds further block on withdrawals from inheritance tax scheme
data.description:
Thousands of pensioners have been hit with a further block on withdrawing their cash from Octopus’s inheritance tax scheme.

The fund, which has 18,000 customers and is known as the Octopus Inheritance Tax Service (OITS), has been frozen to redemptions since early July, meaning savers have been banned from getting their money back.

Octopus was supposed to have reopened the fund either this week or next. However, it said on Thursday that the closure would “need to remain in place for a short additional period”.

OITS, a subsidiary of Octopus Group, had raised money from thousands of pensioners with the promise of lowering their inheritance tax bills by investing in businesses to qualify for relief.

However, the scheme has been plagued by uncertainty in recent weeks after it told savers no withdrawals could take place until it finalised a takeover which risked changing the value of their investments.

Octopus Investments, which administers the scheme, warned customers that while significant progress had been made on the transaction, it still needed to reach a final agreement and the outcome was not “certain”.

The note, authored by Kristy Barr, head of retail investments at Octopus Investments, said: “I know this continued uncertainty is frustrating, particularly for investors who are currently looking to buy or sell shares.

“However, our priorities are to make sure that the outcome of this process and its terms are as favourable as possible for investors and that we maintain our fair and robust valuation and governance process.”

The timeline for the suspension has repeatedly slipped. Financial advisers were told the scheme would be paused for “approximately one week” on July 9.

Later that month, on July 28, investors were told it would be paused for a further six to eight weeks.

Octopus has also faced growing scrutiny about its transparency after The Telegraph revealed that savers had been bankrolling failed hospitals and care homes.

This raised questions about whether pensioners had been given adequate information about the performance of their investments.

Octopus froze the fund over a plan to acquire PlatformX Communications, the wholesale arm of TalkTalk. The deal would trigger a revaluation of the fund, changing the value of customers’ investments.

The deadline for the TalkTalk deal to complete was Friday but this has been extended.

Octopus Investments and TalkTalk said in a joint statement on Thursday that both sides had conducted advanced due diligence and funding was in place.

“As a result, they are optimistic of delivering the proposed transaction and will update stakeholders with further news in due course,” they said. “There can be no certainty of any transaction completing.”

Some investors have become increasingly concerned about the extent of the suspension and the inability to get their money out of the scheme.

Octopus Investments has communicated extensively with customers that have outstanding withdrawal requests, including offering direct phone calls with affected individuals.

Alongside the delay, Octopus Investments also told customers that it was undergoing another valuation of the businesses that make up the investment scheme.

It has completed the process on the part of the portfolio unaffected by the TalkTalk deal, representing about two thirds of the business, with the remaining one third outstanding.

In response to the suspension, Octopus Investments said: “Our priority during this process is securing the best possible outcome for investors and ensuring that all customers are treated fairly.

“We completely understand investors’ frustrations with the ongoing uncertainty but we wouldn’t be pursuing a transaction of this significance if we did not believe it was in the long-term interests of OITS and its shareholders.

“Once we have certainty over how this process will impact valuations, we will communicate with investors and re-open trading as soon as possible. To be clear, the current pause has nothing to do with liquidity: this is currently within historical and expected levels.”

data.title: We must use the remaining fossil fuels to build nuclear. Time is perilously short
data.description:
Britain is trying to replace fossil fuels with weather-dependent energy generation. It is not going well. According to the Government’s own figures, British industry now pays more for electricity than any other International Energy Agency country – a quarter more than Germany and over 60 per cent more than France.

Output of basic iron and steel is down 37 per cent since the start of 2021. Industrial electricity use has fallen in four of the last five years, and is now 13 per cent below its 2021 level – the lowest since 1983. We got rich by making things. We are making fewer of them every year.

In the prevailing narrative, this transition is necessary – to alter the earth’s climate, and to secure our energy supply. The high prices are temporary, an unfortunate combination of badly designed pricing and immature technology.

The remedy is more money, the abandonment of our sovereign oil and gas, and faster deployment of wind and solar. Do that, and we will eventually enjoy abundant, secure, cheap, high-quality energy. We will also lead the world by our example.

Let us grant the concerns about the climate are legitimate. And grant that a supply of inexpensive, reliable, high-quality energy can be scavenged from the wind and sun. The narrative still fails.

It fails because energy is only one of two things fossil fuels give us. The other is raw material. Hydrocarbon is the reducing agent that strips oxygen from iron ore to make steel – a chemical reaction, not a source of heat. It is restructured, molecule by molecule, into plastics. It is the source of the hydrogen in ammonia fertiliser, which feeds about half the world. Every component of a wind turbine – the steel, the plastics, the electronics – is made by burning and consuming hydrocarbons.

As is every component of the equipment that makes the turbine. And when the turbine goes to landfill in 20 years, all of it is required again. There are no affordable industrial-scale processes that replace hydrocarbons with electricity in these applications. Renewable technology is not a substitute for our hydrocarbon system. It is an additional burden on it.

Which brings us to the real problem. That raw material is running out.

“Peak oil” – the prediction that oil supply would rise to a peak in the early 2000s and then fall – goes back to M. King Hubbert in the 1950s. It has been written off ever since, not least because global oil production has kept rising. The dismissal rests on a historical misunderstanding.

The theory is simple. Oil that has not been discovered cannot be produced. So the historical pattern of oil discovery limits the available patterns of future production – “more now, less later” or “less now, more later”, but never “more now, more later”. Global oil discovery peaked in the 1960s and has trended down ever since.

By 2024, new discoveries had fallen to 6 per cent of annual production. From that, simple statistics allow the total discoverable volume to be estimated from that falling discovery curve. And then simple maths allows the shape and timing of production from that volume to be predicted. That shape is a peak.

The maths holds until the economics change. In 2008, they did. Peak oil always meant peak economic oil, the oil worth the cost of lifting it; nobody at the time thought the qualification necessary. Peaking economic oil drove its price to $147 a barrel, and that broke the financial system at its weakest point.

The crisis was answered with credit. Central banks created $28tn, global debt nearly doubled to $348tn and a significant quantity found its way into the petroleum system. Drilling at a loss and refinancing pulled economic oil forward and mobilised volumes that had never been economic, most notably US tight oil. The mechanism held.

What has kept oil volumes rising since has been the uneconomic kind, while the economic stock dwindled underneath it. We do need an energy transition, but not because of the weather – because the supply of economic oil is contracting.

Every successful energy transition in history has met two conditions. The new source was better than the old one – more energy from less material and less land. And there was a large surplus of the old fuel still available, enough to build the new system and keep everyone alive while it was built.

Wood to coal and coal to oil met both. This transition fails both. Wind and sun are diffuse, and they arrive when the weather decides. Everything that follows comes from those two facts. The land, the steel, the concrete and the copper all scale with how thinly the energy is spread; the cost and engineering scale with how much of the time it is absent.

To make a weather-dependent system behave like a dispatchable one, you must build additional capacity to store energy and fill the gaps. That makes the system more complex because wind and solar cannot provide reliable power on demand.

And our hydrocarbon system is contracting, so the second condition fails too: there is no surplus, and we are spending what remains on a system that cannot do the job. Every barrel that goes into it is a barrel unavailable to build something that can.

A time will come when there is not enough energy left to build the replacement – like being 60 miles from a petrol station with 50 miles in the tank.

We have been there before. Transitions have failed, and when they have, people have died – of hunger, of cold, and of the disorder that follows.

The alternative is not complicated. Maximise and conserve what fossil fuel is left and reserve it for manufacturing. Abandon the uses that produce nothing. Electrify everything that sensibly can be electrified now. Work out how to electrify the rest.

Nuclear is the only source dense enough to replace fossil fuel, and the only one we could build with what hydrocarbon remains. Strip away the regulation designed to strangle it, settle the waste question, and build at speed. We must spend what is left on the thing that works.

Richard Lyon is a petroleum engineer, electrical engineer and energy economist. His book The Energy Trap is published by Swift Press on Sept 24

data.title: Hundred-year-old construction giant to stop building homes in UK
data.description:
A 100-year-old construction giant will halt housebuilding to focus on road and hospital projects, as the property slump continues to take its toll on the sector.

FTSE 250 builder Kier Group said on Tuesday that from 2027 “there will be no investment in new property developments, with capital reallocated to enhance the group’s balance sheet strength”.

Its portfolio includes more than 5,000 homes, with construction under way on seven sites. It has said it will finish these before exiting property development.

Stuart Togwell, the chief executive, said the property group was taking “important steps to strengthen and simplify the business”.

Kier will instead focus on its infrastructure and construction divisions, citing more growth opportunities.

In particular, the company is expecting “significant revenue growth” from its water, energy, defence and healthcare contracts.

One of Britain’s biggest construction groups, Kier designs and builds various projects, including schools, hospitals, highways, energy projects and waterworks.

These include roles on HS2 and the Sizewell C nuclear power station.

A £55m office in Liverpool and a 9,290 sq m warehousing site in Manchester are also among its existing property developments.

The news will deal a setback to Labour’s manifesto pledge to build 1.5 million homes during this parliament – a target thsat Angela Rayner, the Housing Secretary, admitted on Sunday that the Government had a “slim chance” of reaching.

Construction continues to suffer a slump amid persistently high inflation, rising build costs and weak housebuyer demand.

Housebuilder MJ Gleeson swung to a loss and cut jobs on Tuesday as the housing gloom continued to take its toll.

MJ Gleeson made a £2.7m loss in the year ending June 30, blaming “subdued” demand for housing. This compared with a £20.5m profit in the prior year.

Graham Prothero, the chief executive, said demand for homes had been hit by an 11-year high in homes for sale in England, rising mortgage rates, and increasing cost of living pressures.

Mr Prothero added that taxes and red tape were making it harder to build homes profitably. The burdens include a building-safety levy to pay for cladding remediation and new net zero rules.

“It is in the gift of this Government to put the brakes on some of those things,” he said. “Now is a very bad time to be imposing the new building safety levy on us ... and the future home regulations [are coming] next year.

“Do we need to do that right now? Could we postpone that and ease the viability challenge? It would be great if we could get some help in that regard.”

The cost of building a new home has risen by £76,000 since 2020, according to the Home Builders Federation. Mr Prothero said half of this was because of increased taxes and regulation.

Under a restructuring at the housebuilder, the company shed 21 jobs after making 56 redundancies while creating 35 jobs.

The group also shut its East Yorkshire office, pulled out of 12 development sites that it had bought and combined its Greater Manchester and Cumbria operations.

Its housing land pipeline has fallen from 19,638 to 14,927 plots.

Mr Prothero said that the “subdued market may not improve any time soon”, so it was taking a “prudent stance” on managing its cash flows. The builder sold 1,968 homes during the year, up 10pc from the previous year.

“You shouldn’t get the impression there are no buyers out there; there absolutely are,” he said. “And we are focusing on what we can do better in order to win over those buyers.”

data.title: Richard Branson’s plan to make the Eurostar feel like a second-class service
data.description:
Sir Richard Branson’s much touted plan to bring some of the glamour of Virgin Atlantic to his own version of the Eurostar has been derided as a pipe dream by critics.

Overcrowding at St Pancras, a chronic lack of suitable train-maintenance sites and the inevitable mountain of red tape have been viewed as almost insurmountable obstacles to anyone intent on ending Eurostar’s monopoly over services through the Channel tunnel.

But after securing permission to run 20 trains a day between London and the Continent from Britain’s rail regulator, the billionaire’s Virgin Trains is finally beginning to win over doubters.

Virgin must still negotiate access to the tunnel itself, as well as tracks in France, Belgium and the Netherlands. And it faces a nervous wait for a fleet of 12 as yet untested high-speed trains on order from manufacturer Alstom.

However, a ruling from regulators at the Office of Rail and Road (ORR) last week suggests Sir Richard may be about to make good on his ambition of returning to Britain’s railways after Virgin Trains lost the West Coast Main Line franchise in 2019.

Virgin Trains is not the only operator intent on challenging Eurostar’s 31-year monopoly.

Italy’s state-owned Trenitalia announced earlier this month a €2bn (£1.7bn) order for 19 new trains, around half of which it aims to deploy on Channel tunnel services, while a clutch of other would-be operators are also drawing up proposals.

If those plans come to fruition, competition on the route could explode within five years, which could have an impact matching that of the 1990s discount-airline boom.

Plunging fares may encourage an influx of new customers and further loosen the grip of airlines on routes such as London to Paris, where Eurostar already has 80pc of the market.

Train services from London are likely to reach further into Europe, with lower ticket prices making rail competitive as far as Germany, Switzerland and even Italy for travellers with time on their hands.

Mark Smith, a former ORR and Department for Transport executive who runs the Man in Seat 61 travel website, reckons ticket prices could drop by close to a third.

“You’d be looking at more capacity, higher service standards and fares that could be 30pc lower based on what we have seen with the advent of competition in Italy and Spain,” he says.

“That will in turn drive further market share gains for rail compared with the airlines and make it feasible to travel further into Europe on a single ticket.”

Customer service front and centre

Virgin has so far been tight-lipped on what the Channel tunnel service might look like, with Phil Whittingham, its project lead, saying only that the route is “ripe for change” and that Sir Richard intended to build a “premium customer experience on board”.

A spokesman adds: “We don’t want to ruin the element of surprise, but just as we’ve done with Virgin Atlantic and our holidays and hotels offering, you can expect bold ideas with the customer experience front and centre.”

On Virgin Atlantic, that experience has included in-flight bar and massages, with a shift to focusing on tech innovation in recent years, including free Wi-Fi from Elon Musk’s Starlink and an AI-powered virtual concierge.

Virgin has specified single-decker trains for its purchase from Alstom, with one insider suggesting that they were more compatible with providing a full at-seat meal service than the double-deckers with which Eurostar is renewing its fleet.

Virgin has said it intends to operate an initial six return trains a day between London and Paris starting in October 2030, later increasing to 13, followed by four to Brussels and three to Amsterdam.

That would represent a substantial increase on the current timetable, with Eurostar offering 14 daily services to Paris, eight or nine to Brussels and five to Amsterdam.

The company, owned by French state railway SNCF, said Virgin’s plan confirmed “the huge potential for growth in international rail” and that it intended to “play a full part in that growth”.

Jon Worth, an expert in European railways, says Virgin had impressed with its work to secure access to St Pancras, the line to the tunnel and the last remaining space at Temple Mills maintenance shed near Stratford before Trenitalia.

“Seeing this project through has been like threading the eye of a needle,” he adds. “Forget the rhetoric from Branson about transforming travel. They’ve been very methodical and very clear headed in devising a project that will just about fit with all these restrictions.”

No room for slippage

However, he says Virgin had taken a risk in choosing a bespoke version of a train built by Alstom in Italy which has not yet been approved in France, introducing the “nightmare” scenario of the trains not being ready for 2030.

Any slippage could open the door to Trenitalia, which is viewed as among the most aggressive of European high-speed operators.

Trenitalia’s train order, from Hitachi Rail, adds to an existing commitment with the Japanese manufacturer and will provide guaranteed delivery times, potentially beating Virgin to the market by a year.

Worth says Trenitalia is likely to expand on routes such as Paris to Lyon and Marseilles and Milan, rather than focusing on London.

Eurostar’s switch to double-deckers for an order of up to 50 new trains may also be problematic, he adds, since the Celestia model is not currently compliant with evacuation requirements within the tunnel in the event of fire.

It is likely that a significant number of the new trains will instead be used on the Paris-Brussels route that Eurostar took over in 2022, easing the pressure on Virgin.

Waiting in the wings are Evolyn, backed by Spanish industrialist Jorge Cosmen, an investor in the owner of National Express, the Dutch startup Heuro, and UK-based Gemini, which has proposed running trains from Stratford and Ebbsfleet to avoid the St Pancras bottleneck.

According to Smith, of the Man in Seat 61 website, Virgin’s best bet will be to play to its strengths by offering upmarket food and wine, exploring initiatives such as allowing carriage of bicycles and dogs, which is currently banned from most Eurostar services.

He says: “It’s that hard-to-define Virgin pizazz that people most want to see and they’ll need to bring that to these trains.”

data.title: Mirror publisher blames ‘expansionist BBC’ as it cuts 220 jobs
data.description:
Reach blamed an “expansionist BBC” as the publisher cut 220 jobs and axed three local online news sites.

The media group – which owns The Mirror, The Express and hundreds of regional titles – told staff on Tuesday that it was making the cuts across its newsrooms and closing Kent Live, Aberdeen Live and Galway Beo.

David Higgerson, the chief content officer of Reach, told staff in an email that “an expansionist BBC” was putting the company under strain.

“Locally, we continue to be challenged by an expansionist BBC, whose local output mirrors what is already being created by publishers up to 70pc of the time,” Mr Higgerson said.

“These headwinds and others which also affect the whole industry mean that we need to make these changes while also reducing our overall costs.”

While Reach will cut 220 journalism jobs, it will create around 60 new ones.

The decision to close the three news sites was because of strong competition from rival newspapers in Kent, Aberdeen and Galway, Mr Higgerson added in the email.

Reach announced earlier this year that it would be moving away from so-called “volume” journalism – a codeword for ad-driven clickbait content – to focus on original, high-quality output.

The company, formerly known as Trinity Mirror, has already begun rolling out paywalls across some of its sites and now has around 50,000 paid subscribers. It has insisted it will refocus on distinctive, quality material.

Algorithm changes by tech giants such as Facebook and Google, which play an essential role in driving traffic to Reach websites, have also hit the company’s financial position.

This has been exacerbated by the rollout of AI overviews that further divert readers away from news sites.

In his email to staff, Mr Higgerson acknowledged that page views had fallen primarily because of a decline in Google referrals.

Several months ago, the publisher said that Google referrals plunged by 55pc in the first half of the year, contributing to a 40pc decline in readership. After its half-year results, shares in Reach plunged by nearly 25pc.

The company has cut more than 1,000 jobs in the past three years. It is now worth roughly £127m, down from a peak of £5bn in 2005. The cuts were first reported by the Prolific North news site.

Reach and the BBC were contacted for comment.

data.title: Founder of collapsed shadow bank ‘gambled millions at Mayfair casinos’
data.description:
The founder of a collapsed British shadow bank spent millions in Mayfair’s casinos.

Paresh Raja, who led Market Financial Solutions (MFS), was a prolific gambler at two prominent Mayfair casinos, the Palm Beach Casino and the Colony Club, according to an individual familiar with Mr Raja’s gambling.

MFS collapsed earlier this year amid accusations of a £1.3bn fraud.

Mr Raja and his wife allegedly received more than £408m from “funds managed by MFS” to “personal bank accounts” in the UK, Monaco, Singapore and the United Arab Emirates, according to a separate lawsuit made on behalf of some of the shadow bank’s creditors.

He is also accused of buying “a vast number of cars” including three Aston Martins, two Mercedes, six Ferraris and three Rolls-Royces.

Mr Raja denies wrongdoing and has consistently maintained that there was no fraud or dishonesty.

According to an individual familiar with Mr Raja’s gambling, the founder would regularly bet up to £60,000 a spin on roulette tables and had a debit card approved by the casinos to be drawn down up to £600,000 per day to gamble with.

This was unusual even by the standards of casinos in Mayfair. As the UK emerged from lockdown, Mr Raja had nearly £1m deposited with the casinos in Mayfair, which were owned by Genting, a Malaysian conglomerate.

The conglomerate has more than 50 casinos in three continents, many of which are in the UK, it has also diversified into other activities including power generation and plantations.

The individual familiar with Mr Raja’s gambling said: “He would come in midweek with a couple of guys that worked with him. These were nice chaps but sort of flunkies, sycophants, let-the-boss-win-at-golf kind of thing.

“He would play and play, drink and drink, and if he didn’t lose all his money at the Palm Beach, he would then get in a car and go around the corner to the Colony Club.”

MFS fell into administration in February, triggering allegations that at least £1.3bn has been “misappropriated” from the business.

Mr Raja was hit by a worldwide freezing order earlier this year, which barred him from spending more than £5,000 a week without creditors’ consent.

The company described itself as a specialist provider of buy-to-let mortgage lending and bridging finance.

It was part of a fast-growing crop of so-called bridging lenders in the UK. These firms provide short-term, property-backed loans to borrowers who may not qualify for traditional bank financing. They often charge higher interest rates.

The property lender boasted a loan book of roughly £2.5bn as of last March and its customers spanned the breadth of the UK.

Its clients included property investors and overseas family offices as well as prominent businessmen and celebrities in Britain.

It was also a shadow bank, which meant it funded its loans by borrowing from banks and other lenders.

The company’s creditors included Barclays, Santander, Wells Fargo and Jefferies. Private capital firms including Apollo’s Atlas SP Partners and Castlelake also extended financing to the failed mortgage lender.

A spokesman for Mr Raja said: “Mr Raja will not comment on a personal vilification campaign.”

Genting was contacted for comment.

data.title: Warren Buffett to step down from Berkshire Hathaway after six decades
data.description:
Warren Buffett is to step down from Berkshire Hathaway, ending one of the most storied careers in investment history.

The 96-year-old, nicknamed the Oracle of Omaha for his market-beating returns, will take on the honorary title of chairman emeritus at the company he bought in 1965.

Mr Buffett quit as chief executive of Berkshire Hathaway earlier this year, making way for Greg Abel, the company’s vice chairman.

He announced on Friday that he will also step down as chairman and will be succeeded by his son Howard, who has spent 33 years as a director in the business.

Mr Buffett said: “Serving as your chairman has been the privilege of a lifetime, and I have never taken your trust for granted.

“Father Time always wins. He has, however, been generous with me.

“He has given me the opportunity to see Berkshire reach a point where I am more confident than ever about what lies ahead.

“The company is in excellent hands, and I look forward to remaining a shareholder alongside you.”

Berkshire Hathaway, based in Omaha, Nebraska, has delivered extraordinary returns for investors since it was acquired by Mr Buffett more than six decades ago.

It has averaged an annual return of 19.8pc, compared to the S&P 500’s 10.2pc.

Mr Buffett owns 13.7pc of the company, giving him a net worth of $145bn (£108bn), making him the world’s 10th-richest person.

Mr Abel said: “Warren’s impact on Berkshire and its owners is without parallel in the history of American business.

“The culture Warren built and the values he championed will remain at the heart of Berkshire, and Howard will be their guardian.”

While investors had long speculated about when Mr Buffett would retire, he shocked them last May with the news that he was stepping down as boss, two years after the death of his long-time right-hand man, Charlie Munger.

Announcing his retirement, Mr Buffett said on Friday: “From the beginning, Charlie and I looked for owners who thought in decades rather than quarters, and we were fortunate to find a great many of you.

“Recently, I celebrated my 96th birthday with family and friends, including one of my great-grandchildren, who had just turned one. He’s moving a bit faster than I am these days.

“I have served Berkshire since 1965. Sixty-plus years in, I still have the best job in the world. That is not something many people my age can say, and I have never felt better about what comes next.

“Part of the reason is Greg. My expectations for him were sky-high from the start, and he has exceeded them. He has taken hold of the chief executive officer job in every respect.

“He has been making the decisions that matter for some time now, and I have not had to think twice about any of them.”

data.title: Burnham faces backlash over Thames Water nationalisation rethink
data.description:
Andy Burnham is facing a backlash from Labour MPs after reportedly shelving plans to place Thames Water into emergency administration.

Backbenchers have urged the Prime Minister to “hold his nerve” over proposals to put the debt-laden water company into a special administration regime, a type of nationalisation.

Mr Burnham has been a fierce critic of Thames Water and has previously said it should be nationalised. He has also frequently promised to bring Britain’s utilities under greater public control.

However, officials have raised concerns about the cost of a possible administration to the taxpayer, as well as the prospect of legal challenges from rival bidders for Thames Water.

The Government is now working on whether there is a viable alternative for putting the utility into administration, with a decision unlikely for several months, according to The Times.

The prospect of Mr Burnham putting the group into administration is looking increasingly slim, according to the report.

The Government’s apparent reticence in bringing Thames into public ownership sparked a furious response from Labour backbenchers.

Jon Trickett, the MP for Normanton and Hemsworth, said: “Privatisation of water has been a disaster. It’s a natural monopoly.

“Worse still, management has proved to be less than competent. Andy Burnham should hold his nerve and stick to his promise.”

Kim Johnson, the Labour MP for Liverpool Riverside, said: “The Prime Minister’s priorities are wrong here.

“Thames Water has been a byword for failure, underinvestment and mismanagement. If we allow it to carry on failing customers with no meaningful consequences, what message does that send?

“This summer has shown just how serious the risk of water shortages is. Public ownership cannot come quick enough.”

The Treasury could face a bill of about £2bn if Thames Water is put into special administration regime, reflecting the funding the company says it needs to remain operational until the end of next year.

Any administration would allow the firm, which supplies about 16 million customers across London and southern England, to continue providing essential services while a long-term buyer was found.

Zack Polanski, the Green Party leader, also urged the Prime Minister to bring the water industry into public ownership. He said: “Privatised water has ripped us off for far too long.

“Sky-high bills. Water shortages. Polluted rivers. Sewage in the sea.

“No more hesitation, no half measures – we need water in public hands now.”

Mr Burnham’s rethink is likely to be welcomed by Thames Water’s creditors, who have been scrambling to secure control of the utility with a proposed £10bn restructuring.

The company has been struggling under a £20bn debt pile and risks running out of cash as soon as October.

Its lenders lined up four new board directors on Monday as part of a potential clear-out of its existing leadership.

The proposed new board would include Mike McTighe, the Openreach chairman, Liz Barber, the former Yorkshire Water chief executive, Clive Selley, the former Openreach chief executive and Dame Bernadette Kelly, a former permanent secretary at the Department for Transport.

Under a 10-year turnaround plan, the new investors said they would take no dividends for a decade or until Thames Water returned to the stock market with a London listing.

Thames Water’s ageing network has been under renewed pressure from one of the driest summers on record.

It has been battling more than 1,000 leaks every week as the clay soil in the ground dries out and causes pipes to crack.

A government source insisted that all options were on the table amid talks with creditors.
