data.title: The West is hooked on Chinese drugs but they could save your life
data.description:
Sir Keir Starmer’s decision to invite Sir Pascal Soriot, AstraZeneca’s chief executive, to Beijing at the beginning of the year was a textbook piece of modern diplomacy.

The then-prime minister’s attempt to revive economic cooperation rested on a knockout deal that went beyond the usual warm words. Sir Pascal, a sworn Sinophile and one of the biggest cheerleaders of Chinese innovation, was only too happy to oblige.

Within hours of Sir Keir’s arrival, AstraZeneca had unveiled a plan to invest $15bn (£11bn) in China, building on its existing medical manufacturing and research capabilities in Beijing, Shanghai, Wuxi, Taizhou and Qingdao.

AstraZeneca’s pledge was the marquee announcement of Sir Keir’s trip. Sir Pascal said the “landmark investment” marked the next chapter for the company in China. For the politburo, it was further proof that their plan to turn China into a global pharmaceuticals leader has worked.

In the West, China has long been dismissed as little more than a dealer in cheap copycat medicines – both legal and illegal – and increasingly knockoffs too, such as unlicensed GLP-1 weight loss medication.

This portrayal no longer bears scrutiny, however. In recent years, the Chinese pharmaceutical industry has undergone a remarkable reinvention. Western industry leaders view it as a bona fide drug superpower at the forefront of discovery.

China controls an exciting pipeline of groundbreaking medicines and occupies a growing role as a globally important venue for clinical trials.

But for now, cooperation between East and West suits both sides. European and American drugmakers have rushed to embrace Chinese research, forging multi-billion licensing deals. Those with the appetite have opened their own labs and even set up manufacturing outposts.

Chinese science is now “the best in the world” and ignoring it is not an option, says one European pharmaceuticals chairman.

Few have led the charge as enthusiastically as Sir Pascal, AstraZeneca’s swashbuckling French boss. China is now its second-biggest market. Meanwhile GSK, the UK’s other national drug champion, has struck a series of partnerships with Chinese labs to licence promising drugs outside the country.

These relationships are critical for China’s pharmaceuticals industry, providing access to the lucrative markets that fund innovation. At home, their only customer is Xi Jinping, and he sets the price.

Yet this partnership is fragile. Amid growing concern in the US about the threat China’s new scientific prowess poses to drug supplies, innovation and even national security, industry executives fear an iron curtain will be drawn.

Drugs may be the next front in the superpower trade war that has already drawn in telecoms equipment, semiconductors, electric vehicles, rare earth minerals and solar panels.

For Europe, including Britain’s pharmaceutical giants AstraZeneca and GSK, the looming nightmare is that an American administration will sooner or later use its economic muscle to effectively outlaw their cooperation with China.

One senior figure says the possibility of a sweeping American crackdown is “probably the one question that keeps me awake at night”.

China’s rapid scientific progress

Dr Zhao Hong, a renowned Chinese cancer specialist, shocked thousands of Communist Party delegates in March last year: a Guangzhou-based biotech firm had developed a cancer drug that had outperformed the world’s bestselling equivalent in clinical trials.

The work of China’s Akeso Biopharma, lung cancer drug ivonescimab had shown that it could delay non-small-cell lung cancer progression for five months longer than US giant Merck’s Keytruda treatment – the world’s bestselling prescription drug in 2025.

The success of ivonescimab was hailed as a breakthrough moment for China’s pharmaceutical industry.

“China is at the best time of its biopharmaceutical sector’s development,” Hong told state media at the annual Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference.

The speed with which China is catching up in pharmaceuticals and biotech is astonishing.

By 2024, China had 1,255 drugs at the research stage, a nearly eight-fold jump in less than a decade. America had 1,441 – a 15pc rise – while the total in Europe had shrunk slightly to 400.

Experts attribute the leap to a fundamental shift in how the industry was perceived by the Chinese regime.

One veteran UK executive recalls how when he first used to visit China in the late 1990s, it was to complain about “counterfeits and pharmaceuticals that were really dangerous”. Today, China is seen as “a golden opportunity”, he says.

“They have moved deliberately to be at the leading edge of science,” he adds.

Beijing has provided vast support in the form of scores of state-financed biotechnology parks equipped with advanced laboratories and heavily subsidised hardware, together with a sweeping overhaul of the regulatory system beginning in 2015.

A study by Prof Yimin Cui, of Peking University, and colleagues found that the time taken to approve a drug for human trials fell to 87 days after the reforms, from 501 days previously.

Chinese researchers are helped by the sheer size of the country’s population – last counted at more than 1.4 billion – says Freddy Yip, a corporate lawyer at Cooley.

“In the US, it may take a long time to recruit sufficient patients, but in China, you have access to lots of different patients with different kinds of diseases, including many rare diseases,” Yip says.

Sir Pascal has said this combination of scientific capability and rapid execution – “China speed”, as he has called it – can help to dramatically accelerate drug development.

One of China’s leading biotech venture capitalists estimates clinical trials are “two thirds cheaper and half as quick in China”.

Progress has been spurred by a massive increase in spending on research and development – leaping from $35m in 2015 to $15bn in 2023 – and a “reverse brain drain” in which thousands of foreign-educated Chinese scientists and entrepreneurs have returned home, according to Porsche Consulting.

Chinese scientists are now at the vanguard of treatment for cardiovascular diseases and cancer, as well as spearheading drug development for metabolic conditions and neurological disorders, such as Parkinson’s, among many others.

Alarm bells in Washington

Mere months before Sir Pascal was lending heft to Sir Keir’s Beijing bridge-building mission, the Frenchman was being warmly welcomed at the Oval Office by Donald Trump.

Thanking the US president for welcoming him “in this beautiful office”, Sir Pascal was armed with another crowd-pleasing announcement: a pledge to cut drug prescription prices in the US, after Trump had accused other countries of “freeloading” at the expense of Americans.

Sir Pascal went further as well, unveiling a $50bn plan to expand the company’s existing operations in the US. In return, AstraZeneca received a three-year exemption from tariffs.

Privately, AstraZeneca executives acknowledge it was also an attempt to ward off growing concern in the White House about the deepening of ties with China.

“We are cognisant of some of the more hawkish commentary [from US politicians]. It is a delicate balancing act, and we are treading a fine line by recognising what the US is trying to achieve,” an insider says.

Yet, for all Washington’s alarm, dependency has become more pronounced, not less. Western companies have piled into the country, hoovering up clinical trial data and striking licensing deals to develop Chinese medicines outside the mainland, which they hope can then be used to treat patients across the developed world.

“This is the golden age of science and China is white-hot right now,” an industry source says.

Deal activity is being driven by anxiety among European and US companies as their pipeline of drugs peters out.

America’s biotech industry faces the alarming prospect of an estimated $350bn worth of medicines – equivalent to roughly one fifth of projected global prescription-drug revenue – losing patent protection by the end of the decade.

When patents run out, generic rivals are allowed to gatecrash the market, jeopardising sales.

Few have led the way with the verve that AstraZeneca has demonstrated.

Sir Pascal’s Beijing announcement was accompanied by a boast that it had signed 16 global licensing agreements with 15 Chinese partners since 2023 alone – thought to be the most of any overseas pharmaceuticals multi-national.

GSK hasn’t been far behind. Last year, the company struck an alliance with local giant Hengrui Pharma to develop a dozen new medicines outside the mainland. The value of the deal could eventually total $12bn.

The agreements are part of an industry-wide surge in deals totalling $138bn last year – a nearly tenfold jump since 2021 – according to data provider PharmCube. 2026 is expected to be another record.

Deal flow shows little sign of slowing.

A fortnight ago, GSK unveiled a $1.3bn pact with Hutchmed, a Hong Kong-based biopharmaceuticals company with research facilities in Shanghai, for the bulk of the licensing rights to what it called “first in-class” cancer treatments.

Brewing geopolitical storm

Amid the feeding frenzy, concern in Washington has turned to outright hostility in some quarters.

In December last year, Trump signed into law the Biosecure Act, a move widely seen as a sharp escalation in tensions and the moment the longstanding strategic rivalry between the US and China spilt into the biotechnology arena.

The act prevents US companies reliant on federal contracts and funding from working with Chinese biotech firms with ties to the Chinese military and any deemed to pose a national security risk. It also bars Chinese companies from accessing US government funding themselves.

US biotechnology companies with federal contracts are now engaged in a mad dash to purge their supply chains of equipment obtained from any Chinese biotechnology firms on the banned list.

Next up is the Biotech Investment National Security Act. Though not yet signed into law, it will subject licensing deals involving Chinese companies to national security reviews.

Though technically a screening mechanism rather than a ban on licensing Chinese drugs, it will effectively function as one, says Craig Garthwaite, a professor at Northwestern University’s Kellogg School of Management.

There is also pressure to bar the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) from accepting Chinese trial data, amid concerns about their reliability. The FDA has repeatedly rejected one of Hengrui’s cancer drugs, citing questions about quality control at its manufacturing sites.

As one senior City figure puts it: the White House has conjured up other reasons to “erect a wall around China”.

AstraZeneca’s attempt to navigate this geopolitical storm by investing in both China and the US divides opinion. Some see it as an inspired way to keep both Washington and Beijing happy at the same time.

“I think Pascal has been very smart in not allowing anybody to question his US credentials. He’s playing his cards very wisely,” the boss of a rival company says.

Others see it as a high-stakes gamble from a company that is more exposed than most of its competitors and has learnt the hard way the risks that come from operating in China.

Leon Wang, the former head of its Chinese operations, is awaiting trial on charges of illegal trading, unlawful collection of personal information and medical insurance fraud, alongside another former employee, having been arrested in 2024.

If the saga made Sir Pascal reconsider his appetite for doing business in China, there is little sign of it.

Alongside licensing deals potentially worth tens of billions of dollars, it has around 17,000 employees in China, two “global strategic” research and development centres in Beijing and Shanghai, and four advanced manufacturing sites in Wuxi, Taizhou, Qingdao and Beijing.

China is now AstraZeneca’s second-largest market after the US, accounting for roughly 12pc of the company’s global turnover, and its Chinese facilities supply more than 70 markets worldwide.

In a written submission to the Commons business and trade select committee in July, AstraZeneca described co-operation with China as a “win-win”.

But as one investor with extensive interests in China points out: “If you’re a big pharma company with a significant proportion of your licensing spend coming from China and the tap suddenly gets turned off, that’s obviously a problem.”

Europe’s wary response

Despite sharply rising tensions, there are concerns that European policymakers are still a long way off from having a coherent industrial strategy that addresses the China question.

Having been slow to react to the threat that cheap Chinese manufacturing poses to the continent’s steelmakers, solar panel producers and its car industry, the risk is that the pendulum swings too far the other way and Brussels takes a similarly antagonistic approach in trying to shut China out of other sectors, such as pharmaceuticals.

Calls by Oliver Blume, the chief executive of Volkswagen, for tougher trade measures against Beijing have been interpreted in some circles as a signal that EU-China relations are close to a tipping point after years of resistance to anti-Chinese duties from the continent’s car giants.

Yet, a senior industrialist says Europe lacks the “economic counterweight to be able to exclude China”.

“I don’t necessarily think it’s good in the long term for the US to do so, but I think it’s very dangerous for Europe,” he adds.

“We need a more nuanced industrial strategy that seeks Chinese expertise and cost effectiveness, and to somehow bring some of the economic benefit of that into Europe,” he says.

Such sentiment echoes a growing willingness among car manufacturers to partner with Chinese counterparts amid an onslaught of imports. Nissan’s decision to share its Sunderland plant with Chery, one of China’s largest car exporters, is expected to be among the first of many similar tie-ups.

Some believe the growing divide between Washington and Beijing because of pharmaceuticals may even present an opportunity for Europe.

“I’m sure Europe would be more than happy to take Chinese-developed products that are sold to them at a lower price than what they might otherwise get from the United States,” Garthwaite says.

As Brussels bureaucrats try to agree on a co-ordinated approach, the rhetoric, particularly among some influential Republicans, continues to harden.

Chris Klomp, a top lieutenant of Robert F Kennedy Jr, the US health secretary, has likened the situation to “a war”.

Anxiety has been heightened by a so-called “hot mic” incident at a Beijing military parade late last year, in which Vladimir Putin and Xi were overheard discussing the possibility that humans could live to 150 years old, thanks to advances in biotechnology.

Some China hawks saw it as further evidence that the US risked falling behind in the global race for domination in advanced science.

The Council on Foreign Relations, an influential American think tank, has called for reliance on China’s biotech know-how to be treated as a strategic vulnerability akin to critical minerals.

“The US (and just about every other nation) faces a growing risk that China will deliberately withhold essential pharmaceutical inputs as a tool of economic or political coercion … as China has done with rare-earth critical minerals,” it warned in June.

The Atlantic Council, another US think tank with a history of shaping American foreign policy, points out that the US is reliant on China for three quarters of some imported drugs and as much as 99pc of some raw materials that are critical to the production of certain key medicines.

What’s more, China’s 2020 export control law and 2021 biosecurity law “grant broad authority to weaponise pharmaceutical exports”, it said recently.

‘All in or all out’

AstraZeneca declined to comment on its position, but there are signs it is more nervous than it is willing to acknowledge.

It emerged in August that the company had held detailed discussions with American rival Bristol Myers Squibb about a potential £300bn mega-merger.

In seeking to substantially deepen its US footprint, AstraZeneca may have concluded that the best chance it has of escaping any crackdown is if the company can demonstrate it is willing to take action to address Trump’s demands for the “reshoring” of pharmaceutical manufacturing.

Radical corporate restructuring plans have also been explored in China. AstraZeneca previously looked at the possibility of carving out its Chinese business into a separate legal entity and listing it on the Shanghai stock exchange. Though nothing came of those plans, they were seen as an attempt to insulate it from mounting geopolitical tensions.

GSK, meanwhile, sees no reason for such drastic action. Publicly, all a spokesman is willing to say is that it has “a longstanding presence in China, to make sure patients can access our medicines and vaccines”.

“China is also increasingly a source of cutting-edge biopharma innovation, and we have established several important collaborations for potential new treatments in oncology, respiratory, immunology and inflammation,” the spokesman adds.

However, like AstraZeneca, it too has fallen foul of Beijing after the company was engulfed in a bribery scandal in 2014.

GSK was found guilty of bribing Chinese doctors and hospitals to prescribe its medical products and was forced to pay a record $490m fine.

That ordeal prompted GSK bosses to take a much more cautious approach in which its activities were limited to strict licensing deals rather than the asset-heavy approach of others, such as AstraZeneca.

“It [GSK] went through a very difficult time in China. The experience damaged the company immeasurably in terms of its willingness to take risks,” a City source says.

By focusing on developing local collaborations, GSK believes it can still capitalise on the opportunities in China while being “less vulnerable” than rivals who are more “asset-exposed”, an insider explains.

Yet, the same person admits it ultimately boils down to one question: “Are they [China] helping us long-term or are they harming us? And I can’t answer that, which is why we can’t afford to be all in or all out.”

Industry figures hope common sense prevails between the two superpowers.

Garthwaite acknowledges deals that come with potential national security risk should be scrutinised, while attempts to reduce American over-dependence on Chinese antibiotics are also to be applauded.

However, he says the White House needs to distinguish between drug production and drug development, which “shouldn’t be too hard”.

Another investor says patients don’t really care where the drugs come from, “as long as they’re subjected to the same trials”.

In response to a recent US ban on imports of humanoid robots, China’s foreign ministry said: “Protectionism does not make the US more competitive … it will only hurt the interests of US companies and consumers.”﻿

Yet, nor is it in China’s interests to actively undermine American science. Chinese drugmakers simply cannot afford to be shut out of Western markets, particularly the US, experts say.

“China is really vulnerable too. It has to rely on its export machine because it doesn’t have sufficient levels of internal consumption,” one analyst says.

Ultimately, industry sources admit they are at the mercy of an unpredictable Trump administration whose appetite for trade wars shows little sign of waning.

As one boardroom veteran puts it: “It’s akin to walking a tightrope – we’ll continue trying to walk it and hope we stay on.”

data.title: Lime withdraws bikes from London borough after complaints from blind residents
data.description:
Lime has removed its electric bikes from a London borough after the company’s vehicles were accused of endangering blind residents.

The company said it had stopped users from being able to hire e-bikes in Bromley, south-east London, where it was operating without an agreement.

It came after Jason Beal, a resident, said he had had to force his guide dog into a busy road because of the company’s lime green bikes being strewn over the pavement.

Councillors had also threatened to pull Lime’s bikes off the streets and charge the company for the hassle.

Liam Conlon, the area’s MP, raised the matter with Bromley council after Mr Beal contacted him to complain.

Lime’s e-bikes have become ubiquitous in London and a popular way of getting around, but the hundreds of them parked on pavements have been seen by critics as a nuisance.

The company had started offering e-bike hire in the Bromley suburb of Penge in recent weeks, despite not having local approval. 

Lime put this down to a technical issue in which the map for neighbouring Lewisham mistakenly covered parts of Bromley. Councillors said they had “blighted” local areas and caused hazards on pavements.

Simon Fawthrop, of Bromley council, said: “We have already raised concerns with Lime that they appear to be operating without our consent in part of our borough.

“Bromley council have long had misgivings about Lime Bikes and other similar bikes that are quite frankly blighting some areas, where they are strewn across pavements causing multiple hazards.

“The council has not agreed anything with Lime and we call upon them to remove their bikes from our borough forthwith.”

Mr Beal, 53, told the London Standard that bikes parked on the pavement meant he had to walk on the road and listen out for traffic, frightening Caine, his guide dog.

“There have been a number of times the Lime bikes have been parked up or propped up against the tree or left over the pavement,” he said.

“So I’ve got to make a decision to try to take him into the main road. That’s a very frightening experience for myself.”

Lime was recently valued at $1.7bn (£1.3bn) in a US initial public offering.

The company operates bikes and scooters in more than a dozen London boroughs.

It has been blighted by claims of personal injuries caused by the bikes, and said recently that it had set aside $56m for personal injury claims.

Lime apologised to Mr Beal and said that it had suspended bike hiring in the borough until it could agree an approach “with appropriate parking locations”.

data.title: Britain’s gas cliff-edge is drawing dangerously close
data.description:
“Britain will control its own energy rather than depending on markets controlled by petrostates and dictators,” said Ed Miliband just before Labour won the 2024 election.

He was pledging to break the growing grip of countries ranging from Norway and the US to Qatar and Algeria on Britain’s energy supplies. Labour promised to replace imported oil and gas with low-carbon alternatives such as nuclear power, wind farms and solar plants.

Two years later, Britain faces a cliff edge in gas supplies, surging prices and soaring imports. This winter looks bad enough. Centrica’s Rough facility, the UK’s only major gas store, is facing the threat of closure without government support, and European storage levels are at their lowest in years.

Analysts are warning of January price increases on top of the 4pc increase planned in October and the 13pc rise last July.

But in a few years, they warn, the situation could be far worse because the UK’s North Sea output is plummeting faster than ever expected.

Last year the North Sea produced 28 billion cubic metres (bcm) of gas – 41pc of Britain’s needs. But in four years, that will have halved to just 14 bcm. And by 2035 it will more than halve again, to 6 bcm.

That reduction could be mitigated by approving new fields such as Jackdaw and Rosebank – but not by much. And those raw figures, from the North Sea Transition Authority, the government regulator, are increasingly striking fear into the gas industry, energy suppliers and government ministers.

They imply that the UK faces increasingly tough, expensive and potentially cold winters over the next decade, and that Britain’s reliance on petrostates will be greater than ever.

“The gap between demand and supply is widening, and it’s going to widen even further in the coming years,” said Iryna Sereda, the global head of gas and LNG at BloombergNEF. “In 10 years, two thirds of the UK’s gas production will be gone.

“Demand is falling too, but not nearly so fast, which means the UK will become increasingly dependent on imports.

“By 2030 it’s likely to be above 70pc and by 2035, we could be as high as 85pc dependent on imports.”

That growing gap between North Sea supplies and UK demand will have to be filled. The only way to do that is by liquefied natural gas (LNG), all of which will have to be imported.

The US is Britain’s main supplier of LNG, but we also buy increasing amounts from Qatar, Egypt, Algeria, China, Equatorial Guinea and Turkey – all of them authoritarian states. And last year alone LNG imports rose 24pc.

So as North Sea output declines, the UK’s hopes of breaking away from “petrostates and dictators” look likely to go into reverse. How did a country that was once self-reliant in energy end up in such a mess? And have ministers even realised?

Gas stockpile plans

One sign that they are waking up came last month when it emerged that Miatta Fahnbulleh, the new Energy Secretary, is considering plans to acquire a large ship that would become the UK’s newest LNG import terminal.

The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero also confirmed plans to create a government-controlled stockpile of natural gas that could be drawn on in emergencies.

Both schemes recognise that the Government’s plans to reduce our reliance on gas are faltering, leaving the UK at increasing risk of price spikes and shortages.

Recently published North Sea Transition Authority data show the physical reality of the North Sea decline.

The UK has about 172 offshore gas fields operating in 2026, but by 2030 around 62 are scheduled to close, leaving just 110. By 2035, another 40 will be gone.

Some of that decline is natural. The North Sea is a mature basin, and output was gently falling by about 5pc a year up until 2022.

But after Rishi Sunak’s government adopted Miliband’s policy of a windfall tax, the annual decline surged to around 15pc as offshore operators scrambled to quit the North Sea.

That could get even worse. If, for example, John Healey carries out his threat to extend the windfall tax, many more North Sea fields would become uneconomic and shut down.

But it’s not just the UK’s own North Sea decline that it should be worrying about.

‘Norway is vital’

Norway, the supplier of about a third of the UK’s gas, is facing the same problem of natural decline.

Britain’s gas needs are not constant. They rise and fall with the seasons. But in the winter, when demand is highest, up to 90pc of the gas burnt in the UK is Norwegian.

That reliance is becoming a problem. A report from the Norwegian Offshore Directorate warns that Norway’s oil and gas supplies peaked last year at around 230 bcm and are expected to plummet to as low as 110 million cubic metres by 2035.

Nikolai Astrup, a Norwegian MP and a key figure on its parliament’s finance committee, said the UK should already be looking for new energy sources. He says: “Right now, Norway is Europe’s largest and most predictable supplier of gas, and all the gas and oil we produce is sold to the UK and Europe. Norway is therefore vital to European energy security.

“But it is a geological fact that the Norwegian Shelf is mature and that the fall in production will be very sharp from 2035 onwards.”

One solution is to reduce demand – an approach recommended by Seb Kennedy, of market data specialist Energy Flux. He argues that building more LNG import facilities would make the UK unhealthily reliant on imports.

He says: “Rather than expanding LNG import facilities, the UK should focus on measures that reduce demand, such as fast-tracking heat pump deployment, investing in heat networks and supporting homeowners with insulation costs.”

That sounds like a solution – until you look at the latest government data. Forecasts of falling gas demand are based on householders installing 600,000 heat pumps a year, mostly to replace old boilers.

But the reality is that 125,000 heat pumps were sold per year, only 7pc of the heating market, dwarfed by the 1.7 million gas and oil boilers purchased.

Gas consumption has fallen in other areas – but not necessarily in ways that benefit Britain. Industrial consumption has plummeted from 19 bcm in 2000 to 8 bcm last year – linked to the closure of thousands of factories.

But the reductions in demand from those shutdowns – and the corresponding displacement of gas-fired power generation by renewables – are nowhere near as fast as the looming decline in UK and Norwegian supplies.

‘Increasingly fragile’

ICIS, a commodity-market consultancy, has modelled the risks posed by this growing gas supply and warns that the winter of 2028-29 is when the threat could become real.

Organisations such as the National Energy System Operator always point to the UK’s diverse gas-supply sources as its best defences.

Those sources include North Sea output, piped imports from Norway, three LNG terminals, interconnector pipelines with Belgium and the Netherlands, and storage.

But ICIS analysis points out that with three of those sources in decline – the North Sea, Norway and storage – the UK is at increasing risk.

“Great Britain’s and Ireland’s security of gas supply becomes increasingly fragile under a declining trajectory of UK natural gas production,” it says.

“Under normal conditions, peak demand can be met, with spare capacity remaining ... In reality, however, each supply source is exposed to planned and unplanned outages.

“The loss of Norwegian imports, or the shutdown of either of the UK’s two large LNG terminals (Isle of Grain or South Hook) significantly reduces available supply.

“If this happens, supply fails to meet demand, not only on the peak demand day but also on multiple days across both the 2028-2029 winter and the preceding winter.”

Some experts say the UK’s and Norway’s decline in gas production matters little because global LNG supplies are growing fast enough to replace it.

David Luff, of Argus Media, said: “Over the next five years, UK gas production is expected to decline faster than consumption, increasing the reliance on imports. But this import dependence will coincide with a significant expansion in global LNG supply, driven primarily by new export capacity in North America and Qatar.”

“Ofgem backs that up. LNG imports will play an important balancing role, although competition for cargoes could intensify if global markets tighten,” said a spokesman.

In other words, far from breaking free from petrostates, Britain will become increasingly reliant on them.

data.title: Net zero grid upgrades drive a £200bn energy industry civil war
data.description:
The subsea cable known as Eastern Green Link 1 will slip into the water at Torness, east of Edinburgh, before resurfacing near the coastal town of Seaham, County Durham.

It is often referred to as a “bootstrap” by energy insiders. But that doesn’t do the project’s scale justice.

Developers say that by 2029 the 120-mile electricity “superhighway” will help unlock Scotland’s renewable energy reserves by transporting enough power for two million homes southward.

At an estimated cost of £2.5bn, it is probably one of the most expensive infrastructure schemes you’ve never heard of – perhaps because it lacks the visibility of a railway, road or bridge.

Yet amid severe delays and escalating costs, Eastern Green Link 1 and schemes like it are now beginning to attract more attention.

The cable and its sister project, Eastern Green Link 2, were originally meant to cost a combined £3.4bn, a figure that has since doubled to an estimated £6.8bn.

Elsewhere, some grid-improvement schemes have already seen their projected budgets balloon by nearly 500pc.

Against the backdrop of a wider £200bn upgrade under way across Britain’s power network, critics fear that it risks becoming a fresh HS2-style fiasco for the Government, with millions of households and businesses left to pick up the tab.

“This is going to make HS2 look like a slick, well-executed operation,” one worried energy industry source says.

Sam Richards, the chief executive of Britain Remade, a clean energy pressure group, adds: “The simple truth is that Britain is building too much grid, at too high a price.”

Squeeze on household bills

Britain’s power grid is an engineering marvel. It spans 530,000 miles of cables, including some 10,000 miles of high-voltage transmission lines – the motorways of the system – and another 520,000 miles of lower-voltage distribution networks that carry power to people’s homes.

It was largely built through the 1950s, ’60s and ’70s and designed to manage power for a highly centralised system that depended on a relatively small number of coal-fired and nuclear power stations.

But to reach net zero carbon emissions, significant changes are required.

In a system dominated by renewable-energy generators, such as wind and solar farms, the network will instead rely on a large number of smaller power plants scattered across the country.

Along with a need to modernise infrastructure, the “great grid upgrade” set in train under successive Labour and Conservative governments is driven largely by net zero.

In total, it is expected to trigger more than £200bn of investment across distribution, transmission and interconnectors between this year and 2040, according to consultancy Baringa.

This includes £68bn alone to expand the UK’s transmission grid, the high-voltage cables that carry power over long distances to cities.

Households and businesses ultimately pay for all this work through their energy bills, which are rising to fund it.

According to tracker website Electricitybills.uk, the network component of a typical household’s bill is on course to have risen by 65pc, or from £207 to £342 per year, between 2025 and 2030.

Contrary to the oft-repeated mantra of Labour ministers, this means network charges, rather than volatile gas prices, are currently the biggest driver of domestic bill increases.

At the same time, modelling by SQE Energy suggests most industrial and commercial businesses face increases of between 60pc and 90pc in transmission network charges over the next few years.

“If you put it all together, including new expenditure and what you have to spend on ‘catch-up’ refurbishment of assets that should really have taken place previously, it’s a huge number – probably our biggest infrastructure undertaking as a country at the moment,” says Nick Forrest, a partner at Baringa.

Yet despite the vast scale of spending – and the outsized impact it is having on bills – energy suppliers including EDF and Octopus Energy say the grid upgrade programme has been rammed through with little scrutiny or regard to the costs it will impose on their customers.

One reason they are concerned is that polling shows consumers will probably blame them – rather than grid companies – for the ever-growing bills landing on their doormats.

But like HS2, there are also concerns about complicated regulatory processes.

“It’s f------ impenetrable,” complains one executive at a major energy company.

“You have to live and breathe this stuff to really understand it. We weren’t happy with the way it was pushed through.”

Another insider described it as “opaque and undemocratic”.

And what is now ringing further alarm bells is a string of delays and cost increases that threaten to push the cost of the grid-upgrade programme even higher.

Along with the Eastern Green Link cable schemes, several major projects are reporting surging cost inflation.

For example, a report quietly published by Ofgem in May revealed that a string of eight projects being built in Scotland by SSE were forecasting total cost increases of 284pc on average.

This included a staggering 467pc projected cost increase for work to upgrade transmission lines between Loch Buidhe and Spittal.

Ofgem has not disclosed the potential cost of the overruns in cash terms, or what their impact could be on bills.

But the available figures are not encouraging.

Another one of the eight projects is a high-voltage subsea cable between Spittal and Peterhead.

The exact cost of this individual link remains guarded, but SSE recently awarded a mammoth €2bn (£1.7bn) combined contract to Danish manufacturer NKT to supply cables for both the Spittal-Peterhead route and a separate Western Isles link.

Ofgem analysis reveals the Spittal-Peterhead scheme’s estimated overall budget has increased by 111pc since initial projections.

This has led to the watchdog allowing SSE to spend more on early construction costs, but it is still deciding whether any further increases are reasonable.

Crippling production bottlenecks

The regulator has said it will “rigorously challenge” all cost rises, but its past record is weak and experts fear it will have little grounds to challenge companies for higher spending that is being driven by external factors.

“There are lots of factors in the control of the transmission and distribution companies, but there are also quite a lot of things outside of their control, from the time it takes to get planning approvals to global supply chains,” says Baringa’s Forrest.

For example, Ofgem announced in 2022 that the Eastern Green Link 1 and 2 projects would cost a combined £3.4bn.

But when the developers of the scheme went to the market to secure the materials and services they needed, they found the costs were far higher than expected.

Ofgem was reluctantly approving a budget of £4.3bn alone by 2024 for Eastern Green Link 2 – after managing to find just £67m of spending it deemed unnecessary.

The surging costs have been blamed on the global rush towards renewables, which has sent prices for grid equipment surging as countries around the world all try to buy the same things at once.

According to the International Energy Agency, the cost of cables and transformers surged 91pc and 72pc higher between 2019 and 2024, with manufacturers also taking longer to deliver as they battle production bottlenecks.

Any kind of delay is a nightmare for developers, because it forces them to pay contractors for longer or spend more on storing equipment until it is needed.

But understanding exactly what is driving costs can be difficult because of a paucity of publicly available information, says Ed Hezlet, an energy expert at Onward, a Right-leaning think tank.

In many cases, National Grid and other companies are allowed to keep the finances of individual schemes hidden because they are deemed “commercially sensitive”.

“There’s evidence that costs have shifted up very significantly since 2022, but it’s hard to really know what’s going on,” Hezlet says.

“That’s worrying, because if you take the HS2 analogy, you definitely want to find out if something’s massively running over budget early rather than later – so you can actually talk about it properly and address it.

“Ultimately, billpayers are going to be footing the bill for all of this. So there should be far more transparency about both the cost and the progress of these projects.”

‘Limited amount of information’

EDF, one of Britain’s biggest energy suppliers, has also warned that there is currently a lack of transparency about both the scale and cause of the cost increases, not all of which can be pinned on inflation alone.

The company claims it is “impossible” to fully assess how bad things are based on “the limited amount of information available”, but adds: “There has been substantial supply chain cost inflation over the past few years, and this is likely to continue as countries across the globe tackle the same electricity network and generation challenges.

“We estimate costs have risen two or three times since initial transmission operator forecasts. This is corroborated by our own experience of connection cost increases for our generation projects.”

At the same time, it says, generators seeking to connect to the grid are facing average delays of two years – meaning the extensive upgrade work being undertaken may not actually be needed as quickly as thought.

Taken together, EDF and others argue this should prompt a rethink about whether the money being spent on grid projects is still good value.

“If we want to change direction, now is the last moment where this is possible without creating significant sunk costs, or delaying projects that are much-needed within the system,” EDF added.

In response, the Energy Networks Association lobby group insists the upgrade will deliver value for money.

In fact, Lawrence Slade, the group’s chief executive, says: “Network investment is supporting the connection of more affordable and reliable homegrown energy – it is an ongoing process that is creating thousands of jobs today, strengthening our long-term energy independence and ensuring customers will save on their bills in the future.

“Ofgem has stated that transmission network investment is expected to lead to around £80 of savings for bill payers by 2031 compared to not investing, which means bills are expected to be around £30 lower than they would have been had investment not been made.”

An Ofgem spokesman added: “While upgrades will requires upfront investment, failing to invest would also increase costs for consumers through higher constraint and balancing payments caused by grid bottlenecks.”

But just how far behind is Britain’s “great grid upgrade”?

Some of the best clues come from documents published by the National Energy System Operator (Neso), which is tasked with managing the grid day-to-day.

Of some 90 projects deemed essential for Labour’s clean power target, 64 have delivery dates falling after the all-important year 2030.

Among them is Eastern Green Link 2, which Neso says is needed by 2029. Instead, it is not on course to connect until December 2035.

Similarly the Beauly-Denny upgrade in the Highlands is needed by 2029 on Neso’s own numbers, but has substation works attached to it dated as late as November 2036.

The Telegraph sent questions to the Government, Neso, grid companies and trade bodies at the heart of the grid upgrade asking about the surging delays, cost overruns and the effect on bills. All refused to give detailed answers.

Kayte O’Neill, the chief operating officer at Neso, insisted that documents published by the quango did not represent a “Clean Power 2030 delivery tracker”.

However, she admits that delivering a decarbonised grid by 2030, the political target demanded by Labour in 2024, is proving challenging.

“Neso has consistently advised that delivering clean power by 2030 is a significant challenge,” she says.

“Achieving it will require cross-sector collaboration, including accelerated delivery of critical network infrastructure from transmission owners, implementation of connections reform and continued coordination between industry, government and Ofgem.”

A spokesman for the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero said: “We are reversing decades of underinvestment in the grid, alongside the private sector, to build an energy system that can bring down bills for good.”

Chris Bowden, the chief executive of SQE Energy, a supplier that manages grid connections for businesses, says the cost overruns and delays were already showing up in the data.

He argues that the cost of reaching Labour’s target in just four years will be huge – especially for industry and business, which are largely unprotected from price rises.

Bowden says: “On bills, the domestic impact gets most of the attention, but the industrial and commercial side is larger and less discussed.

“Our modelling suggests most industrial and commercial businesses face increases of 60-90pc in transmission network charges over the next few years.”

The chief executive adds: “One client’s charges are set to more than double to over £17m by 2029.”

With such substantial cost increases coming down the pipeline, some critics now argue that the Government should press pause on major grid spending until it can be sure everything planned is needed.

For example, Greg Jackson, the boss of Octopus Energy, Britain’s biggest energy supplier, has argued that new technologies, such as AI and dynamic line rating, which can help to squeeze more capacity out of existing power lines, should be exploited fully before consumers are tapped for costly upgrades.

He has also argued that major market reforms, such as switching from Britain’s current national electricity pricing system to a series of smaller, more localised markets, could remove the need for such massive works by forcing energy companies to be more efficient.

This is because energy producers will be encouraged to build out power suppliers in different parts of the country to support local markets, removing the need to transport energy from north to south.

In an interview with The Telegraph this year, Jackson suggested that this change could invalidate tens of billions of pounds currently set to be spent on grid upgrades.

A report produced this year for Octopus by FTI Consulting, a lobbying group, suggested that moving to locational pricing would render between £22bn and £30bn of planned transmission upgrades unnecessary.

This would potentially unlock between £55bn and £73bn in consumer bill savings between 2030 and 2050, it said.

Richards, at Britain Remade, agrees. “The way to reduce the amount of grid infrastructure that’s needed is by switching to local pricing.

“By cutting bills where the power is generated, more will get used at source, cutting the amount of wires and pylons needed.

“On top of this, planning delays, vexatious legal challenges and excessive regulation on new energy infrastructure is driving up grid build costs.

“Continuing to reform the planning system is essential if the Government is to deliver on its pledge to reduce energy bills.”

Doing so, he argues, will be essential if Andy Burnham, the Prime Minister, is also to meet his promise to put more money into voters’ pockets.

Onward’s Hezlet also fears that failing to reappraise grid costs now could have painful and long-lasting consequences.

“There’s good reason to be concerned because this stuff is basically going to be locked into our bills for 45 years,” he says.

Chris O’Shea, the boss of British Gas owner Centrica, is also concerned.

He argues that Burnham should consider moving more of the grid upgrade costs off bills and into general taxation – a prospect that may have little appeal as John Healey, the Chancellor, grapples with existing black holes in his Budget.

“Upgrading Britain’s energy networks is essential if we’re going to build the low-carbon, secure energy system the country needs,” O’Shea says. “But we must be honest about how that investment is paid for.”

The boss of British Gas adds: “Loading too much of the cost onto bills risks putting more pressure on households and making life harder for businesses, particularly smaller firms that are the backbone of the economy and already facing tough conditions.

“Major infrastructure investment is best funded through general taxation, which is fairer, more transparent and better reflects the national importance of these upgrades.”

So far, however, ministers have proved reluctant to back down on their grid spending splurge.

Miatta Fahnbulleh, the Energy Secretary, said in a recent radio interview with LBC that the upgrade work was a necessity.

“I don’t think, if we did not invest in the infrastructure of our energy system, anyone would forgive us,” she said.

“It is not a choice to make sure that we are upgrading our energy system. We absolutely need to do that.”

As bills surge, households are unlikely to forgive Labour for the alternative either.

data.title: Nationalise Thames Water to block hedge fund takeover, MPs urge
data.description:
Andy Burnham should immediately take control of Thames Water to prevent hedge funds from seizing it, MPs have urged.

The embattled utility company faces takeover by its lenders under a £10bn rescue deal, but MPs have urged the Government to act before that happens.

Alistair Carmichael, the Liberal Democrat MP who chairs the environment select committee, said: “Thames Water’s 16 million customers have largely lost faith.

“We do not believe this opaque consortium of 100 hedge funds has the interests of the public, the company or the environment at heart.”

The committee has called on the Government to push ahead with a so-called “special administration regime”. This form of nationalisation would see officials and the water regulator, Ofwat, appoint an administrator to manage the business.

The company could then be restructured, and the Government could find a new approved buyer.

The MPs called on the Government to bring in emergency legislation to push through the administration “to draw a line under this debacle and restore stability to the sector”.

Thames is struggling under a debt pile of almost £20bn and has admitted that it faces running out of cash by the end of the year.

A group of more than 100 lenders, known as London & Valley Water, includes US hedge funds Elliott Investment Management, Silver Point and Apollo.

As part of the £10bn deal, London & Valley Water has said it will inject billions of pounds into the business to fund upgrades to Britain’s ageing water network.

It has also committed to paying out no dividends until 2035 and offered the Government a “golden share” in the business.

Mr Burnham indicated that he would explore bringing Thames into public ownership. However, Thames’s advisers have suggested that this could cost £4bn and officials have raised concerns about the cost of the process.

Mr Carmichael said the cost of placing the company into special administration would be “neutral to the taxpayer” if the investors, whom he alleged had lent money to Thames “at payday-lender rates”, were not compensated.

He called on the Government to reject any further offers from the company’s current creditors.

The MPs added that Ofwat’s current special administration rules were too vague and appeared to trigger only if the business collapsed.

They called for the public takeover to be “triggered earlier” or for “fresh legislation” to push the company into special administration.

The committee also criticised Thames’s current environmental performance and customer service.

A Thames Water spokesman said: “Turning Thames Water around will take a decade and require significant and sustained investment, but we are already making progress, and this is a different business from the one it was two years ago.

“We are delivering the biggest upgrade of our infrastructure in 150 years, and we are seeing the benefits of that investment.”

A spokesman for the lenders said: “All profits will be reinvested, and no dividends will be taken until the company is turned around and returned to the public markets. There will be no cost to the Government or taxpayers, and customers will be protected from the costs of Thames Water’s restructuring.”

data.title: Boohoo chairman quits after battle with Mike Ashley
data.description:
Boohoo has announced the sudden departure of its chairman, a year after Mike Ashley accused him of ignoring investors’ best interests.

The online retailer announced on Friday that Tim Morris will step down from his role with immediate effect.

His exit comes a little more than a year after Mr Ashley’s Frasers Group wrote to Mr Morris threatening to hold a shareholder vote over his position.

Frasers, Boohoo’s biggest shareholder, sought to eject Mr Morris after it struck a loan deal that Mr Ashley’s representatives claimed was damaging to the business.

Boohoo, which trades as Debenhams Group following a rebranding last year, risks a fresh row with Mr Ashley after it said on Friday that Iain McDonald, a former director, would return as executive chairman following Mr Morris’s departure.

Mr McDonald had remained a significant shareholder in the business and was also accused by Mr Ashley of governance failures.

Mr McDonald’s reappointment has prompted an analyst to drop its coverage of Debenhams, who called it “the antithesis of progression” given that he had served on the board between June 2017 and February 2026.

Clive Black, the vice-chairman of City broker Shore Capital, said: “The missed opportunity of evolving the board with fresh, new talent, is frustrating, to our minds, which leads us, sadly, to conclude that Debenhams’ share price will not fulfil the ultimate potential of the firm, a distinctive and remarkable position.”

Mr Morris joined the company’s board in May 2021 and was made chairman in November 2024.

Under his tenure, the company suffered a major shareholder revolt amid criticism over millions of pounds in bonuses paid to bosses last year. More than 40pc of investors voted against Boohoo’s remuneration report in a significant rebuke last September.

That was a month after Mr Morris came under fire from billionaire retail tycoon Mr Ashley following the announcement of a £175m borrowing facility for Boohoo, which carried an interest rate of 7.3pc above the Bank of England base rate.

Frasers had offered a month earlier to provide financing at what it called “substantially more favourable terms”. Mr Ashley’s company offered Boohoo a £125m loan facility with an interest rate of 2.5pc above the base rate.

In the letter to Mr Morris, Mr Ashley’s lawyers said: “How is it in the best interests of Boohoo, its shareholders and its other stakeholders for so much money to be sucked out of the Boohoo group, when cheaper financing was available?

“Throughout this period, you have ignored the requests for a meeting, you have ignored the potential for synergies with Frasers and you have ignored the superior financing offer made by Frasers.

“Because you have led Boohoo to a very expensive financing while ignoring a far better proposal from Frasers, you should expect a shareholder meeting for a vote on your personal position on the Boohoo board.”

The departure of Mr Morris is the latest chapter in the long-running tensions between Mr Ashley and Boohoo, led by rival tycoon Mahmud Kamani. The pair first clashed in 2021 when Boohoo beat Frasers in a battle to control Debenhams.

Frasers owns a near-27pc stake in Boohoo, built up after the latter company beat Mr Ashley to buy Debenhams out of administration.

Announcing his departure, Mr Morris said: “It has been a privilege to chair this business through such a pivotal period.”

Dan Finley, the chief executive of Debenhams, said: “I would like to thank Tim for the significant and critical contribution that he has made to our turnaround.

“The business has been significantly strengthened during his tenure as chair. We wish him all the very best in his future endeavours.”

His replacement, Mr McDonald, added: “It was a very difficult decision to step away from the board of Debenhams earlier this year, and it is a great honour to be asked to return in the role of chair.

“I am a material investor both personally and via the funds managed by my business, Belerion Capital Group, and this is a measure of the degree to which I believe in the potential of the business.

“The progress made over the past six to 12 months is significant and there is a real feeling of momentum in the business. I look forward to supporting the management team in their efforts to restore value and to engage constructively with all shareholders.”

data.title: Revolut eyes stock market listings in London and New York
data.description:
Revolut is plotting a dual stock market listing in London and New York.

The digital bank, valued at $115bn (£85bn), has previously shied away from committing to a UK float. However, Nik Storonsky, its founder, said it was considering the London Stock Exchange (LSE) for the first time on Thursday.

Such a move would be a major boost for the UK market, which has been hit by an exodus of companies and a drought of new listings.

Vue, the cinema chain, is also exploring plans to list on the LSE, its chief executive Tim Richards told the Financial Times. He said there was “too much gloom” around the London market and hoped to debut its shares in the UK.

A London float of Revolut would make it one of Britain’s largest listed companies, putting it on a par with FTSE 100 giants including Barclays, BP and GSK.

Mr Storonsky said that although Revolut would list in London, he still wanted it to have a presence on Wall Street “because it’s a larger market”.

He said: “We have the choice between selling in a small market with few buyers, or in a gigantic market with a huge number of buyers who will compete fiercely for our shares. Therefore, yes, we prefer the United States.

“In reality, we are currently planning a dual listing, on the London Stock Exchange and the Nasdaq.

“If you truly have a strong brand in the United States, with a popular and accessible product, your customers will also participate in the [initial public offering], which will have a positive effect on our market capitalisation.”

UK ‘less liquid’

Mr Storonsky has previously dismissed the possibility of a London float, arguing that it was “not rational” to list in Britain because of the 0.5pc stamp duty charged on purchases of shares.

Two years ago, he said: “The UK is less liquid so it’s much worse compared to the US plus it’s much more expensive because you pay stamp duty – it’s just not rational.”

Earlier this year, Mr Storonsky said any listing of Revolut would only happen by 2028 at the earliest. A source close to Revolut said a float would be subject to market conditions.

Mr Storonsky, who was born in Russia, started Revolut in London in 2013. The company has since grown to become one of Europe’s largest and most valuable online banks.

He later renounced his Russian citizenship in 2022 in the wake of Vladimir Putin’s invasion of Ukraine.

Mr Storonsky has previously criticised Britain’s “extremely bureaucratic” regulators, while claiming “it’s hard to do business in the UK”.

Revolut was awarded a full UK banking licence in March this year, having first applied to become a full bank in 2021.

data.title: Global coal demand hits record high as Iran war cuts gas supplies
data.description:
Global coal consumption is set to hit a new record this year as war in the Middle East drives up global gas prices.

The International Energy Agency (IEA) said coal use would rise 1.2pc to a record 8.94 billion tonnes, after previously predicting that demand for the fossil fuel would decline.

The Paris-based agency said high gas prices and demand for air-conditioning, driven by the climate effect of the El Niño weather phenomenon, were pushing up coal consumption.

It linked the surge to the ongoing Iran war.

The agency said: “Although virtually no coal shipments pass through the Strait of Hormuz, the disruption has nonetheless affected coal markets by pushing up natural gas prices due to the plunge in liquefied natural gas shipments through the Strait.

“This has in turn encouraged more coal-fired generation in countries with gas-fired power fleets and spare coal capacity.”

The IEA predicted global demand for coal will “rise above previous expectations amid higher demand from import-dependent countries, such as Japan and Korea”, after global gas prices soared.

It added that this year’s so-called “Godzilla” El Niño weather pattern would lead to more coal demand from countries in Asia, such as India and Vietnam, as high temperatures lead to more demand for air-conditioning and lower hydropower output.

Coal use has been in long-term decline in Western economies as they switch to gas and renewables. However, usage has remained high in many developing economies and China, while Mr Trump has sought to encourage more coal production in the US.

A kilowatt-hour of power generated by burning coal typically releases a kilogram of CO2 – double that of gas. A typical UK household consumes 12,000 kilowatt-hours of energy a year.

The rise in coal use coincides with scientific reports that August was the world’s joint hottest month on record, with global temperatures at 1.65C above pre-industrial times.

Last month was the hottest August on record, with Western Europe experiencing its warmest ever summer, scientists from the EU’s Copernicus Climate Change Service said.

A run of heatwaves from May to August caused droughts in the UK, France, Hungary, Romania and Serbia, with major rivers, such as the Rhine and Danube, seeing exceptionally low flows.

Prof Friederike Otto, who specialises in climate science at Imperial College London, said: “You don’t need to be a climate scientist to see the evidence of climate change; you just need to look out of your window.

“Until we stop burning coal, oil and gas, these record-shattering months will simply keep on coming.”

The IEA said coal demand could increase again next year if the Strait of Hormuz remains closed.

data.title: Burnham to cut energy bills by up to £200 for benefits claimants
data.description:
Andy Burnham is to cut up to £200 off benefits claimants’ energy bills this winter as the Iran war sends gas and fuel prices surging.

The Prime Minister is exploring providing targeted subsidies to millions of households living in fuel poverty including those who do not currently qualify for existing support.

Whitehall officials are understood to have started drawing up the scheme after the outbreak of the US-Iran war put a squeeze on global oil and gas supplies coming out of the Strait of Hormuz trade choke point.

The energy price cap is poised to jump from £1,663 to £1,723 in October, with analysts forecasting that it will rise again to £1,872 in January – a total increase of about £200 across the winter.

The support scheme, called the Energy Price Protection Payment (EPPP), is “ready” to be implemented in January, according to industry insiders. It would aim to mitigate some or all of the impact of the rise in energy prices.

It could be announced as soon as the Budget on Oct 28, or potentially in late November when the next energy price cap adjustment is confirmed.

There are also discussions about whether a wider package of support could be provided to all households but this would be more expensive and could clash with the vow by John Healey, the Chancellor, to protect the public finances.

No final decision has been made yet on whether to proceed with the EPPP or how much the support will be worth.

It would apply to people who already receive the Warm Homes Discount as well as some others deemed in need of support.

To receive the discount, a claimant must be in receipt of benefits. But sources said the support was poorly targeted and did not cover another estimated 2.5 million extra households who were still classed as being in fuel poverty.

It is unclear whether the EPPP would seek to target only some or all of those households.

One person familiar with the plan said it could be part of a wider energy bills intervention that could “layer” support to benefits claimants on top of more universal measures.

However, they stressed the final shape of any package would be determined by the strength of the public finances and how energy prices evolve.

The Iran crisis has sent European gas prices to their highest point since 2022, prompting fresh concerns about the cost of living at a time when Mr Burnham has pledged to put “more money in people’s pockets”.

He has already cut VAT to zero on electricity bills, saving a typical household about £45 per year.

However, the cut has already been wiped out by rising energy costs and is scheduled to expire at the end of March.

Industry sources suggested that the Government was looking at other ways to bring down bills in the long term such as reducing or eliminating network charges and green levies.

Ministers cut bills by £150 for households last year by removing the energy company obligation and 75pc of the renewable obligation in the last Budget.

However, a letter on Friday from more than 120 businesses, trade groups and charities including Nationwide, Octopus Energy and British Gas urged Labour to go further and cut levies by an additional £100 a year.

They said: “Moving electricity levies from both business and household bills to government spending would immediately make energy costs more affordable and competitive, providing a greatly needed boost for our manufacturing industries and tackling cost of living challenges.”

Miatta Fahnbulleh, the Energy Secretary, is also thought to be championing proposals inside the Government for a so-called block tariff. This would grant all households a discounted “block” of electricity and gas, with anything used above that threshold charged at the normal rate.

A government spokesman said: “The Chancellor is fully focused on giving families and businesses breathing space and helping ease cost pressures.”

data.title: Billionaire Brexiteer Crispin Odey’s fall from grace
data.description:
Stooped about the witness box, Crispin Odey was barely audible as he was cross-examined by a lawyer for the City watchdog.

The normally ebullient hedge fund boss, 67, was giving evidence as part of his attempt to overturn a lifetime ban from the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA).

The hearing earlier this year focused on an arcane section of the watchdog’s rule book: whether Odey – who twice fired his executive committee before it could discipline him about allegations he “lacked integrity” – acted “recklessly” and breached its rules.

But everyone in the room knew the subtext to the proceedings: the hedge fund tycoon’s history of alleged sexual misconduct stretching back decades.

Perhaps it was the toxicity of these allegations that made Odey vacillate between proud and evasive when answering questions from the FCA’s chief counsel, Clare Sibson KC.

Asked later by the judge why he chose to close Odey Asset Management (OAM), his eponymous hedge fund, instead of trying to sell his stake, he responded: “I am a proud man.”

This defiance pushed Odey into an expensive legal battle with the City watchdog – one which cast fresh light on repeated allegations of sexual misconduct stretching back decades.

That battle ended in defeat for Odey on Monday. A court upheld a £1.53m fine for the financier – reduced from an initial claim of £1.8m – and a lifetime ban from financial services, ruling in favour of the City watchdog.

The Upper Tribunal, which decides on appeals against the FCA, ruled in its favour, finding Odey had deliberately worked to frustrate an internal investigation into misconduct allegations, while showing “reckless disregard” for City rules.

It said Odey had “repeatedly prioritised his own interests at the expense of risk of detriment to OAM, its staff members and investors” while seeing “nothing wrong with his approach”.

“Mr Odey’s only purpose was self-preservation and to avoid being held to account for his behaviour,” the FCA said.

For many observers, the spectacle of Odey in court laid bare the other side of a man once lauded as one of the “sharpest and most contrarian brains” in the City.

Who is Crispin Odey?

Odey was a rarity among his secretive hedge fund peers, enjoying an outsized and flamboyant public persona.

Born to Yorkshire industrialists, Odey was educated at Harrow and Christ Church, Oxford, where he read history and economics.

After graduating, Odey was handed control of the 4,000-acre Hotham Hall estate that had been in his family for centuries, but was soon forced to sell everything off to settle his father’s substantial debts.

After entering the City, he was briefly married to Rupert Murdoch’s eldest daughter, Prudence, but the relationship only lasted 15 months before they divorced.

Then, in 1991, he married Nichola Pease, a fund manager whose family helped found Barclays, creating a power couple often called the “Posh and Becks” of the City. The same year, Odey set up his eponymous firm, with backing from early investors, including George Soros.

During the ensuing decades, Odey became one of London’s best-known hedge fund tycoons, in part because of his astute ability to cash in on chaos.

The hedge fund boss correctly predicted that the value of insurance companies would rise in the wake of 9/11, before pocketing £28m in 2008 after successfully predicting the financial crisis.

The Brexit-backing financier gained further notoriety among political opponents in 2016 when he made £220m by betting that markets would drop after the referendum result.

“Il mattino ha l’oro in bocca [The morning has gold in its mouth],” Odey said to the BBC on the morning after the vote.

Odey has not been immune to failure. OAM, whose assets under management stood at $13.3bn (£9.8bn) at its peak in 2015, went through volatile shifts in fortune. One of his funds lost 44pc of its value in 19914.

Undoubtedly, though, Odey has done well out of his bets. His pay peaked at £36m in 2010 and he and his wife were estimated to be worth £775m in 2019.

In addition to his own fund, Odey held a significant stake in Sky, which he cashed in after its $39bn takeover by Comcast.

Odey, who in 2010 threatened to leave the UK in protest against high tax rates, has complemented his financial gains with forays into politics. He made political donations valued at £1.7m between 2007 and 2019.

Some went to Boris Johnson and the Conservative Party. More recently he donated to Nigel Farage’s Reform UK. The majority of his donations were channelled into groups campaigning for Brexit.

Odey also captured the imagination with his wholehearted embrace of the rarefied world of Mayfair high finance.

At more than 6ft tall and of ample build, Odey strikes an imposing figure.

Known for his trademark City uniform of red braces, the financier has also been described as a “country gent”, whose passion for enriching himself was rivalled only by his enthusiasm for country pursuits, such as hunting and fishing.

Nor has he shied away from displays of extravagance. He spent more than £130,000 building a Palladian-style chicken coop in 2012, nicknamed “Cluckingham Palace” by the tabloids, at his Gloucestershire estate, Eastbach Court.

The financier, who has a sausage named after him, was also notorious for his prodigious appetite. At one midweek meal with a journalist, he paired steak and kidney pudding and mash with a “side order” of a loin of beef and two bottles of wine.

Odey’s larger-than-life personality contrasted with allegations of a more menacing side. Media reporting and the lengthy dispute with the City watchdog have detailed incidents in which women were allegedly sexually assaulted. In one case, a woman accused him of rape, which he strenuously denied.

His reputation earned him the nickname “the octopus”.

The allegations first emerged publicly in 2020, when Odey was charged with indecent assault on a woman in 1998 after she accused him of groping her in his Chelsea home.

The trial, which came in the wake of the “Me Too” movement, gained significant publicity, with the hedge fund chief pictured leaving court clad in a mask and flanked by his wife.

Odey admitted propositioning the woman, then 26, but denied assault. He was acquitted in 2021, with the judge ruling there were “inconsistencies” in the woman’s account.

Two years later, Tortoise, and then the Financial Times, published investigations outlining allegations that Odey sexually harassed or assaulted 13 women during the course of 25 years.

Odey settled civil claims from five women in May, weeks before they were to be heard in court.

The lawsuits include allegations that Mr Odey raped a woman in the mid-1990s, an accusation he called “wholly false”.

Odey also mounted a £79m defamation claim against the Financial Times, but dropped it in April.

The consequences have already rippled through Odey’s private life. He and Pease, who have three children together, divorced soon after his court case in 2021. Odey has since remarried Diana Vitkova, a Bulgarian-born finance executive 26 years his junior.

Meanwhile, OAM collapsed in 2023 as major banks cut ties and investors pulled their money, forcing the company to start winding down its funds.

‘Playing the victim’

Odey mounted his challenge against the FCA ruling earlier this year, seemingly in an attempt to cling on to what might have remained of his status within the industry.

Yet the hearings in the Upper Tribunal did little to repair his reputation, particularly after he failed to have the sexual harassment claims excluded from the case.

By the end of the hearings, the FCA’s lawyers had accused Odey of submitting “false evidence” to the court and a “brazen” attempt to create a “false history” of events.

“Mr Odey displayed a remarkable absence of self-awareness, was evasive, inconsistent, and had a tendency to attack others whilst playing the victim,” the regulator argued in submissions to the court.

Witness statements and court testimony paint a picture of a working environment controlled by a domineering and at times abusive boss.

Odey Asset Management, which was based in a five-storey Georgian townhouse in Mayfair, operated much like a feudal state, with Odey, controlling 75pc of the fund. He had a reputation for reportedly hiring “earls and girls”, with a predominantly male and former public-school workforce and women hired usually only as receptionists.

The court heard claims that OAM was an “old boys’ club”, with documents suggesting that executives at the firm had “very similar backgrounds” to Mr Odey.

For a string of women at the firm, however, it went far further than a gender imbalance.

OAM commissioned law firm Simmons & Simmons to carry out an investigation in 2020 into its founder’s conduct. The resulting report detailed at least 46 misconduct claims against Odey dating back to 2003.

The court heard one incident in which it was claimed Odey gave a female employee a massage before “groping her breasts”. He was then accused of trying to manipulate the woman “into silence”. The hedge fund boss has blamed his actions on a dental sedative he took earlier that day.

Yet this incident was described as part of a culture of “prolific sexual harassment” that was “accepted as part of the deal” of working at OAM. As one of his former employees testified, Odey was a “sex pest” who found it “hard to control himself” around women.

On the stand, Odey acknowledged staff thought he was a “creepy old man” but defended his behaviour with female subordinates. “Maybe I am a dinosaur; I cannot see how any of that can be sexual harassment,” he said.

Odey argued that the FCA was under “political pressure” and “sought a totemic case”, adding that the watchdog had a “pre-determined view of his fitness and propriety”.

That the allegations took so long to surface has in part been put down to a culture of complicity within OAM. But it was also a result of Odey’s concerted efforts to bury the allegations and oust anyone who threatened to make them public.

‘Evidence of gross misconduct’

After the damning internal report was published in 2021, OAM’s executive committee issued a final written warning to Odey regarding his behaviour. The court heard that it cut Odey’s pay by 40pc, after pressure from the FCA.

It also banned him from physical contact with other staff members, excluding handshaking, and inviting or accompanying any female members of staff to events or shopping trips or contacting them by text or email.

That summer a new allegation surfaced after Odey told a temporary receptionist she should “take a lover”, the court heard, and then accidentally showed her an indecent photo of his girlfriend while sharing pictures from a fishing trip.

The executive committee scheduled a disciplinary hearing in November to consider whether Odey had breached its final warning. But Odey acted first. On Christmas Eve, the tycoon sacked the entire committee – a move described by one witness as the “nuclear option”.

Odey subsequently decided that the disciplinary hearing into his conduct would be indefinitely postponed. He appointed new committee members, but after disagreement about how to proceed with the hearing, he sacked this board as well.

Some of Odey’s former employees tell a story of bullying. In his witness statement, Thomas Richards, OAM’s former chief operating officer and a member of the committee, said the hedge fund boss had called him “f-----g spineless” and threatened to shut down the fund.

Another executive said he felt “physically threatened” by Odey after recommending he work from home or take a sabbatical. Jack Satt, the firm’s compliance chief who resigned in the wake of the scandal, said Odey offered him £1m and a future role as chief executive if he stayed on.

These executives were not beyond reproach. Howard Cornwell, a former FCA official, described the outcome of the initial disciplinary hearing as “unsatisfactory”, saying he believed there was “evidence of gross misconduct which would normally lead to dismissal”.

He said: “Supervision was of the view that OAM’s decision in not removing Mr Odey, as controller and founder of OAM, was motivated in part by self-interest given the potential impact of removing Mr Odey on the firm as a whole.”

But there was no doubting Odey was a force to be reckoned with. The hedge fund tycoon even took an aggressive approach towards the FCA itself, at one point threatening to “go straight to the f-----g press”.

In an explosive outburst to one official at the watchdog, he said: “You will not get away with this – I have an agreement then you little guys, trying to do your work in the shadows ... You are about to create a crisis.”

For now, the City watchdog triumphed. The tribunal ruled against Odey, upholding all five of the FCA’s allegations against the hedge fund manager, including that he threatened the watchdog’s staff.

He has two weeks to file a further appeal.

Instead of restoring his reputation, Odey’s appeals have only caused a deluge of allegations to resurface.

Therese Chambers, the FCA’s executive director of enforcement, said: “During the hearing he reinvented history, painted himself as a victim and displayed no contrition.

“That arrogant entitlement and the resulting complete disregard for proper governance means Mr Odey is unfit to work in financial services.”

And, despite Odey’s claims to the contrary, it is a crisis entirely of his own making.
