data.title: Wind farms accused of pushing up bills by exploiting loophole
data.description:
Wind farm owners have been accused of pushing up household bills by exploiting a “loophole” in green energy subsidies.

The loophole involves contracts for difference (CfDs), the 15- or 20-year fixed-price deals that are handed to wind farms to give developers certainty about their future income.

These are used to underpin the finances of most renewable energy schemes and are ultimately funded through consumer bills.

Ministers have repeatedly described CfDs as good value because they lock in relatively low-priced supplies of power for consumers that can shield them from price increases during crises.

But some developers have repeatedly exploited a rule allowing them to delay the start of their contracts so they can sell power at higher market rates instead. This has allowed some to reap huge windfalls.

Ministers closed the loophole in 2023, but projects awarded CfDs before then can still use it.

One energy executive claimed the situation was an “absolute p---take”.

They accused some developers of “making out like bandits” from the arrangement at the expense of millions of households and businesses, at a time when the US-Iran war has sent power prices surging.

One wind farm, Seagreen, off the coast of Angus, Scotland, is thought to have made about £27m extra by exploiting the loophole in the past two years, according to an analysis of market data by The Telegraph.

The scheme’s first phase secured a CfD in 2019 and construction finished in 2023.

Its CfD had a target start date of March 2025, but this has been repeatedly pushed back, with owners SSE, TotalEnergies and PTTEP now saying that they expect to activate it in March 2027.

There is no suggestion of wrongdoing by the companies, which must activate the CfD by a “hard stop” deadline of September 2028.

Spot power prices in Britain have jumped about £75 per megawatt-hour (MWh) during 2026 and are currently sitting at around £156 per MWh.

This means a wind farm, such as Seagreen, which was awarded a fixed CfD price of about £55 per MWh in today’s prices, can currently reap substantial profits by selling electricity at market rates.

David Turver, an independent energy analyst, argued this went against the spirit of CfDs, which are meant to help support the business cases of wind farms.

He said: “The ability to delay the start of CfDs was originally intended to help developers manage the risk of construction delays.

“But in some cases, the wind farms have been built already and they are simply choosing not to activate the contracts so they can get higher merchant power prices. They are benefitting in that way from higher gas prices.”

The energy executive added: “The CfD bid they made was predicated on what they [would] earn over the period covering construction, plus operations, plus the cost of capital – so the extra earnings now are pure windfall.

“In these times of high energy prices, they make out like bandits before activating it at their discretion.”

The Government previously urged wind farms to “act fairly on this matter, recognising the public support they have received for development”, before closing the loophole in 2023.

A spokesman for Seagreen Wind Energy Limited said on Friday: “In August 2026, we updated the Low Carbon Contracts Company regarding the expected start date for the CfD for Seagreen Phase 1.

“This has been done in accordance with the terms and conditions of the contract.”

data.title: Guardian staff threaten walkout over pay as paper hails record revenues
data.description:
Guardian staff have threatened to walk out in a row over pay as the newspaper hailed its highest-ever revenues.

The National Union of Journalists (NUJ) is to hold an indicative ballot of members over whether to strike in protest against the company’s latest pay offer.

Union bosses said the move followed a “sustained lack of progress” in pay discussions, branding the latest offer “inadequate”.

Staff are in revolt about a proposal to increase salaries by 3.85pc. While the uplift is above inflation, the union said it did not “meaningfully” address cost of living pressures.

Journalists have also complained about increased workloads under editor Katharine Viner’s Project Berger strategy, which includes greater focus on audio and video and expansion in the US and Australia.

On Thursday, The Guardian revealed revenues grew to £282m in its latest financial year, up 2pc and a record for the media group’s news operations.

The newspaper, which does not charge for online subscriptions but asks readers to make one-off or monthly contributions, reported a 17pc increase in reader revenues to £126m last year.

Revenue generated outside the UK rose 8pc to £115m, suggesting the company’s international push is starting to pay off.

Bosses said growth was particularly strong in the US, where the paper now has more than half a million paying readers.

Despite rising revenues, The Guardian, which is owned by the £1.2bn Scott Trust endowment, lost £17m last year, though this narrowed from £24m the previous year.

The newspaper’s resilient performance is likely to further fuel anger among journalists who argue it could afford a more generous pay deal.

The strike ballot, which is open until next Wednesday, is indicative, meaning the union will not be committed to industrial action in the event of a yes vote.

Nevertheless, it underscores the level of discontent at the publisher. The two sides are entering an Acas mediation process.

Restructuring

The prospect of fresh strike action will create a headache for Guardian bosses two years after staff staged a 48-hour walkout in protest against the sale of The Observer to news start-up Tortoise, led by James Harding, the former BBC News boss.

The sale of the Sunday title went ahead despite the strike, and the Scott Trust invested £5m in Tortoise as part of the deal.

However, it opted not to participate in Tortoise’s latest funding round, which closed last month.

The Guardian has separately outlined proposals to stop using “casual” workers and instead create up to 95 new roles.

However, some staff have raised concerns that the newspaper is preparing to employ an army of low-paid young graduates, similar to the model employed by struggling publisher Reach.

A Guardian spokesman said: “Negotiations are ongoing, and we believe we have offered a fair pay increase which is above inflation and compares very favourably with other employers in our sector.

“We are reviewing how we engage with and manage casuals in editorial to ensure the system is better suited to their needs and our operational requirements. We are engaging constructively with the NUJ as we undertake this work.”

data.title: 10 things to do before retirement (or risk your pension falling short)
data.description:
For most of our working lives, retirement can feel like a theoretical concept. But if you have five years or fewer to go until you plan to give up work, it becomes more of a reality.

By that time, your financial position is more certain, and any financial forecasts can be more realistic. This is the key opportunity to check that your plans really are on track and make final decisions.

We’ve enlisted the help of financial planning and retirement experts to explain the important steps to consider.

Five years before retirement

1. Check your state pension entitlement (and fill gaps if appropriate)

Confirm what state pension you will get and when. It is currently in the process of gradually rising to 67, which will be complete by 2028. This could catch out those expecting to start claiming as soon as they turn 66.

Because of how the age rise is being phased in, it means someone who turned 66 in January could start claiming from their 66th birthday, but those born later in the year might face a delay. For example, someone turning 66 on October 1 can only claim once they are 66 and six months old.

Check our state pension age calculator to find out when you can start your claim.

The amount of state pension you are paid is based on your own National Insurance record; it may not be the full rate (currently £12,548 a year), so check yours via the Government Gateway.

If you have gaps in your National Insurance record, it may be worth paying to fill them.

2. Decide whether to use the services of an adviser

Choosing to go it alone or use the services of a financial adviser is something you need to think about and plan for a few years before actually retiring.

Shop around and take your time when it comes to finding an IFA, said Ian Millward of Candid Financial Advice.

“Avoid anything too complex or someone who tries to blind you with science. You need trust – but that shouldn’t be blind trust – and you need to understand the plan. The relationship should feel collaborative.”

Alternatively, the government-backed agency Pension Wise provides free guidance to people from age 50, to help you understand your retirement options. It will tell you what you “could” do, not what you “should” do.

3. Review your investments and ‘lifestyling’ options

There is a tendency to reduce investment risk as you approach retirement. So, with just a few years to go, now is a good time to look at where your pensions are invested and consider whether this is the right level of risk for you.

Some pensions have what is known as “lifestyling” built in, where stock market holdings are automatically reduced in favour of things such as gilts and cash in the years before your nominated retirement age.

However, should gilts crash – as they have in the past – this could leave your savings vulnerable. Plus, you could miss out on growth if you de-risk too early.

“A couple probably have a life expectancy of over 30 years between them [after reaching retirement age] and need the kind of return only the stock market can provide to give them a secure retirement.

“It may sound counter-intuitive but de-risking into retirement can actually be more risky, as being too cautious can lead to you running out of money in old age,” said Mr Millward.

Now may also be the time to consolidate your pensions and have your savings in one place – but only where it makes sense.

Older schemes sometimes have benefits, such as enhanced levels of tax-free cash, guaranteed annuity rates or some old with-profits contracts providing minimum guaranteed returns. These benefits would be lost on transfer.

4. Boost pension savings – it’s not too late

Ideally, by this time you will have saved enough throughout your working life to build a pension pot that can sustain you throughout retirement. However, life can be messy and sometimes it can actually make sense to make larger contributions later in life.

“Often this will be when children are no longer dependent, the mortgage has been paid off and salary is highest,” said Tom Selby, of AJ Bell.

“This is one reason why annual pension contribution limits need to be high and ‘carry forward rules’ are important – it provides flexibility to make up for lost time.”

For example, let’s take a 60-year-old who earns £70,000, has a pension pot worth £300,000 and is in a company pension scheme which pays a total contribution of 10pc (combining employee contribution, employer contribution and tax relief).

If they keep making the same contributions until age 67, they could have a pension worth around £456,000, according to calculations from AJ Bell.

This would generate £114,000 of tax-free cash and a £342,000 taxable pot. If just the taxable part is used to provide an income, they’d be looking at a starting income of around £14,800.

But, add £15,000 (inclusive of tax relief) each year for the final five years they’re in work, on top of their usual contributions, and this pot could be worth around £540,000 when they turn 67.

You’re then talking about tax-free cash of £135,000 and a taxable pot worth £405,000 which, using the same assumptions, could provide an income of around £17,600, increasing by 2pc per year, for around 30 years.

Three years before retirement

5. Request a quote for any final salary pensions

Obtaining accurate information on final salary pensions can be slow and hard to decipher – often telling you what your pension was worth when you left service years ago, but giving little information on what to expect when you need it.

And don’t assume it will be worth more if you defer taking it. “That can be a false calculation as it ignores the income you would have received in the meantime, so do the maths and don’t be shy about taking pensions early if that’s what you need to do,” said Mr Millward.

6. Pay off debt

Clearing debt should be a priority. While borrowing rates have dropped in the past couple of years, they are still much higher than the rock-bottom rates seen in 2022. There’s also potentially huge comfort in being debt-free when you’re no longer working.

7. Build up emergency savings

Volatile markets are challenging even with the security of a job behind you, but the stress can escalate when that regular source of income has gone and, instead of paying in, you are now drawing from your pension.

“Investment returns are notoriously unreliable, so always assume your first year of retirement will coincide with a stock market crash and plan accordingly,” said Mr Millward. “What that really means is: keep a healthy cash float.”

In retirement, you may want to have 12 to 18 months’ expenses in an emergency fund you can freely access. There is no set figure for this – it really boils down to what you need to buy you peace of mind.

One year before retirement

8. Review your outgoings

Costs often fall significantly in retirement; you don’t need to pay to commute, there’s no work wardrobe required and often your children will have flown the nest.

Scrutinise your essential outgoings to try and work out how much you may need each month – a budgeting plan such as the 50/30/20 method or zero-based budgeting could help.

It’s also a good time to review costs such as insurance and utility suppliers to try to reduce prices where you can.

9. Decide on pension options, including deferring your state pension

At this point, you’ll be making final decisions about entering drawdown, buying an annuity or taking ad-hoc lump sums from your pension pot.

When it comes to drawdown, a good rule of thumb on how much you can draw from your pensions and maintain the real value of the capital is generally regarded as around 4pc a year. However, you may need to adjust this figure depending on market performance and inflation, along with other costs that can eat into your pension returns.

The real differentiator here is charges, with most financial advisers charging around 2pc a year, said Mr Millward: “This is an enormous bite out of anyone’s savings.”

“If you are taking 4pc, you need total returns above 6pc a year before you even start protecting the value of your money against inflation,” he added.

“With that level of charges, 3.5pc or even 3pc might be a more realistic withdrawal level. But if you can get total charges down to around 1pc, then 4pc is probably still a realistic starting assumption – and a healthy pay rise for you.”

It’s also possible to defer your state pension in return for a higher guaranteed income later on. Whether this is sensible will depend on several factors, including your health, income sources and spending needs.

10. Factor in the tax issues of part-time working

Deciding when and how to stop working is a deeply personal decision and one of the biggest transitions in our lives. Many people ease their way into retirement by reducing their working hours over time and, in parallel, gradually increasing their pension withdrawals.

Be aware that there will be tax implications if you work while drawing a pension.

The first 25pc of a pension can be taken as a tax-free lump sum, while the rest is viewed as taxable income and subject to income tax.

When added to your other income in the tax year, you may be pushed into a higher tax bracket. This is more likely if you take a large amount from your pension in one go.

Once you start withdrawing money from your pension then the money purchase annual allowance (MPAA) kicks in. This limits the amount of money you can contribute to your pension to £10,000 each tax year.

data.title: Labour’s wealth raid ‘kills off ultra-luxury homes in London’
data.description:
Labour’s wealth tax raid combined with stringent planning laws has effectively killed off ultra-luxury property developments in London, experts have warned.

Branded residences – luxury homes with hotel services – are often viewed as symbols of status and wealth creation.

Some of the UK’s best-known examples include the Mandarin Oriental at One Hyde Park, and the OWO Residences by Raffles in Mayfair.

But a combination of recent planning rules restricting flat sizes, weak demand and Labour’s hostility towards the super-rich has prevented property developers from building them in Britain.

It means a 120-home project in St John’s Wood, scheduled to finish in 2028, is likely to be the last of its kind according to a new report from property consultancy Knight Frank.

Gareth Stow, the chief executive of St John’s Wood Square, said in the report: “It’s probably the last super-prime scheme in London of any scale.”

Planning rules adopted by Westminster city council in 2021 introduced a 200 sq m size limit on new homes, covering neighbourhoods including Mayfair, Belgravia and Knightsbridge.

St John’s Wood Square secured planning consent in 2015, making it the last development of its size that will deliver flats averaging 300 sq m.

But at the same time, wealthy buyers have been scared off by Labour’s tax crackdown on the super-rich.

A number of billionaires have left Britain in protest against higher taxes on investments, inheritance and capital gains, as well as the abolition of non-dom status.

The latest to flee is Chris Rokos, the hedge fund billionaire, who is preparing to move his residency to Greece amid concerns Labour will raise taxes in the upcoming Budget.

“A realignment of capital is under way at the top end of the market,” says Rupert des Forges of Knight Frank.

“A lot of these buyers have reduced what they are going to spend here because of the cost of purchasing and sentiment towards wealth. Everybody is a lot more transient than they used to be.”

The UK’s hostility towards the super-rich has stood in stark contrast to countries such as Italy and Greece, which have instead introduced policies designed to attract more wealthy overseas buyers.

The drop-off in construction has meant that London’s market for branded residences has been outpaced by Dubai, the US and Thailand.

The global market has tripled in a decade, rising from 354 schemes in 2015 to 903 at the end of 2025. The number of projects will exceed 1,000 this year.

The report also shows there is growing buyer appetite for concepts such as longevity clinics, hyperbaric oxygen therapy, cryotherapy, sound-healing studios and other “biohacking-focused” wellness facilities.

A government spokesperson said: “Property markets are influenced by a range of factors, and SDLT forecasts are produced independently by the OBR.

“We are getting on with the job of building the homes this country needs, such as through our Social and Affordable Homes Programme, driving the biggest council housebuilding revival in decades.”

data.title: The Treasury is wasting money and holding back growth
data.description:
In 2003, I was working in the Department for Culture, Media and Sport on the bid for the 2012 London Olympics. My job was to do the planning for if we won.

At the time, conventional wisdom said this was a remote possibility.

The Civil Service’s revealed preference was for us to produce a better bid than Paris, but lose out to the French in the final reckoning, probably because it was assumed they would cheat.

Success all round without the headache of actually having to host the Games.

I really wanted us to win. Alongside setting up the Olympic Delivery Authority and the Organising Committee – a great triumph – I was also responsible for putting together one of the early budgets. Less of a success. We originally estimated the costs would come in at around £4.5bn and it was nearly twice that in the end.

Some of the over-run was owing to complexity. The land was so polluted it cost nearly £250m to wash the soil. Less forgivable was the fact that VAT wasn’t included in the construction costs.

In my defence, I’d only been in the Civil Service for a couple of years by this point and hadn’t been trained in the mysteries of government finances. It wasn’t obvious to me that when setting out the cost to the public purse, the tax to be paid by the Treasury to the Treasury should be included as part of the bill. I went on a training course.

I learned that it is less complicated to include the tax take in calculations of government spending and let the Treasury balance its own books without the help of optimistic young bureaucrats. Simplicity is not always the answer, but there are areas of government spending where a common-sense approach would serve us so much better.

The Treasury classifies the money it spends in four ways. There is “department expenditure limit”, which is the amount of money a government department is allocated to spend in a spending round. There is “annual managed expenditure”, which is the spending in-year that is harder to predict and control, such as the welfare bill or pension payments. Then there is “resource”, day-to-day spending on running costs, such as salaries, and there is “capital”, investment in physical assets that have long-term value.

The dividing lines are not always clean. For example, decades-ahead commitments to public-sector pensions are hidden within everyday spending on salaries.

I always thought of annual managed expenditure as the spoiled child of government finances: spending and more spending, and then coming back for even more. Capital allocations were in contrast made with care and thought for the long-term benefits. Call it two-tier accounting. This disparity is a key reason for the current housing mess.

The taxpayer has been building houses and subsidising accommodation for people who can’t afford to pay for it for centuries. My weekend run goes past handsome Elizabethan alms houses. Assuming that we’re not wiped out by AI, our great-great-grandchildren will still be paying taxes to subsidise housing for those who need it. But hopefully they will be smarter about it.

Last year, the Government spent £37.3bn on housing benefits. This is some of the most unproductive spending even by the standards of our public finances. The bill grows as the cost of renting rises. The cost of renting grows because the supply is so scarce.

The Treasury should make public the actual cost of there not being enough homes and be transparent about how much the failure to build inflates the benefits bill. It costs us all in every sense.

As the chairman of the homelessness charity Shelter, you’d expect me to say there must be homes to rent for people who have been priced out of the housing market. You would expect me to argue that people who are vulnerable and need help should have a secure roof over their heads, even though we haven’t built enough houses.

Even without that moral argument, however, the economic case for the Government building houses is made. It is better value to build decent homes than to continue to pay too much for not enough. Housebuilding would support construction and provide decent homes for the 177,000 children who don’t have one and avoid the social, economic and human consequences that risks.

Public money can be spent so much more productively. There’s more to be done to stimulate private investment too. Legal and General has shown that affordable housing can provide a stable long-term returns. The key to unlocking more capital is for the Treasury to more fairly compare its profligate day-to-day spending with investment that pays back.

In the end, the London Olympic Games cost £8.9bn of public subsidy. Even the most conservative estimates put the return to the UK economy as at least twice that. It’s the difference between investing and spending.

data.title: Air traffic control took hours to seek help over flight chaos glitch
data.description:
Britain’s air traffic control service waited almost three hours before seeking help to fix a software glitch that grounded more than 2,000 flights.

A preliminary report from National Air Traffic Services (Nats), which controls flights over the UK, said on Friday that the initial error that caused the meltdown was detected as early as 10am on Sept 8.

On-site engineers studied the issue for two and a half hours before the glitch triggered a meltdown in the main flight data system responsible for tracking planes in UK airspace, leaving an estimated 330,000 passengers stranded.

The engineers were not initially aware of the severity of the problem. Only at nearly 1pm did they contact the firm responsible for maintaining the software and request additional specialist support, the report said.

By then flights had been halted, marking the start of six hours of chaos at airports across Britain.

The Government has ordered an investigation into the travel disruption amid questions about why the software issue was not diagnosed before the chaos began.

Heidi Alexander, the Transport Secretary, said: “It’s clear we need to urgently understand why this issue was not discovered and fixed before it caused chaos.

“I have therefore tasked the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) with conducting an independent review to check Nats’ findings and investigate their investment plans to enhance resilience in the future, along with regulatory accountability.”

It is understood that the CAA has been told to complete the review within six months.

The disclosure that Nats knew about the software issue but failed to solve it faster will raise questions about the future of Martin Rolfe, the firm’s embattled chief.

Airlines, including Ryanair, have called for the Government, which holds a golden share in Nats, to dismiss Mr Rolfe after a succession of IT failures at the control service, including one in August 2023 that left 7,000 passengers stranded.

Mr Rolfe has apologised for the incident, while adding that the report showed it was unrelated to the 2023 outage and that Nats has invested more than £1bn in improving its systems and technology.

Airlines UK, which represents the major carriers, said it would write to Nats to demand “immediate compensation for the costs incurred and a credible plan to improve resilience”.

Tim Alderslade, who heads the lobby group, said: “Passengers don’t need more hollow apologies or empty promises that lessons will be learned.

“They deserve commitment and proof that the system is being fixed. The CAA’s review must mandate real investment in Nats’ resilience so a single fault can never again descend into nationwide disruption.”

The Nats report revealed that the meltdown had been traced to software that allocates four digit codes, known as “squawk codes”, to help identify individual aircraft on radar.

While one request for a code was being processed, the system received another deemed to be higher priority. However, when it returned to the first item the software defect meant that it did not process it correctly, introducing a glitch into the system.

The report said the error in a small subsection of coding had not previously caused problems because requests had never before overlapped to within a thousandth of a second.

It said: “For the fault to occur, a higher-priority request had to arrive during that exact millisecond while the original request was part-way through updating a value.

“Had the higher-priority request arrived even one millisecond earlier or later, the update would have completed normally.”

Nats said the glitch initially triggered a rupture just after 10am that lasted for 45 seconds before links were restored.

Engineers ruled out a hardware problem and were working to understood what had gone wrong when the system crashed again 90 minutes later.

Once again it came back on line before repeatedly failing and finally losing the connection completely after another hour.

Flights were first halted at 12.45pm, though Nats did not hold a call to brief airlines and airports on the situation for a further 55 minutes.

While only those flights above 24,500ft supervised from the London area control centre were directly affected, restrictions had to be placed across the UK so that the system could be rebooted and flight data reloaded.

data.title: Post Office chief joins high street undertaker firm
data.description:
A former Post Office chief who had to hand back a bonus for his work on the inquiry into the Horizon IT scandal has a role at an investment firm known for swooping on struggling retailers.

Nick Read, who was chief executive of the Post Office from 2019 to 2025, has been made an operating partner at Modella Capital.

Modella has scooped up brands that have subsequently struggled after being bought, including TG Jones (formerly WH Smith), Claire’s Accessories and the Original Factory Shop.

The former army officer joined Modella as an “operating partner” in the summer and is now listed on its website.

According to Sky News, Mr Read is being lined up for a boardroom role at another Modella investment, Flying Tiger Copenhagen, a variety retailer that trades from more than 1,000 locations, including many in the UK.

Mr Read succeeded disgraced former Post Office chief executive Paula Vennells in 2019 after running grocery chain Nisa.

It was during his period at the Post Office that the enormous scale of the Horizon scandal, which resulted in wrongful fraud convictions for hundreds of postmasters, was fully revealed.

In August 2023, Mr Read was forced to apologise after admitting he had received a £455,000 bonus on top of his annual pay, of which an amount was linked to his work supporting the public inquiry into the Horizon scandal.

He later handed back the portion of the bonus related to the enquiry.

In April 2024, the Post Office’s former chief people officer Jane Davies told MPs that Mr Read had repeatedly threatened to resign over his remuneration between 2022 and 2023 and said he was “obsessed” with pay, a suggestion he denied.

Modella acquired TG Jones, the rebadged former WH Smith high street stores chain, in April 2025 for £42m. It is currently in the throes of a huge financial restructuring to stave off insolvency .

Modella also bought Claire’s Accessories from administrators last year before closing all 154 of its standalone stores in April.

Another purchase, discount chain the Original Factory Shop, also went into administration and shut down its operations earlier this year.

Modella is one of the potential bidders for the discount chain Poundland, which has been put up for sale by Gordon Brothers. It was also said to be interested in buying the luxury department store Harvey Nichols, which was eventually acquired by Sports Direct owner Frasers.

Modella declined to comment on Mr Read’s involvement.

data.title: Channel 4 to axe 300 jobs in biggest ever round of cuts
data.description:
Channel 4 is expected to cut around a quarter of its workforce in the biggest redundancy round in its four-decade history.

Priya Dogra, the broadcaster’s new chief executive, is expected to confirm the cuts as part of a broader strategy on Wednesday at an all-staff meeting.

Channel 4 is still finalising numbers, but the cuts will affect between 300 and 325 roles, The Guardian reported. A spokesman declined to comment, saying staff would be informed of the measures first.

Layoffs of that scale would represent about 25pc of the broadcaster’s workforce, which stood at 1,276 last year. It would mark the deepest cuts in the history of Channel 4, which was founded under Margaret Thatcher in 1982. It last announced 240 job losses two years ago.

The youth-focused broadcaster is attempting to shore up its finances as it undertakes a difficult shift to the digital era.

It has faced an exodus of younger viewers to streaming and social media rivals such as Netflix and YouTube and has struggled to reverse a decline in ad revenues from traditional TV.

The company fell into a £10m deficit last year – its third consecutive year in the red – though losses narrowed.

Ms Dogra, who replaced Alex Mahon as chief executive in March, has been reviewing Channel 4’s structure and strategy.

The company, which is publicly owned but commercially funded, secured permission from the Government this summer to access the remaining half of a £150m debt facility to ease its financial pressure.

It is unclear which roles will be affected by the latest cuts, but London could face significant losses, as the broadcaster has outlined plans to sell and move out of its Westminster offices.

Bosses have also pledged to increase jobs in the nations and regions after opening a new headquarters in Leeds.

Ms Dogra could also seek to shake up Channel 4’s commissioning strategy to win back audiences. The broadcaster has been spending less on new programming in recent years to keep a lid on costs.

Ian Katz, Channel 4’s head of programmes, will step down next month after nearly nine years in the role.

Mr Katz, the group’s longest-serving content chief, is credited with discovering shows such as Taskmaster. However, Channel 4 has faced criticism for being too reliant on old hits, such as Gogglebox and The Great British Bake Off.

Jonathan Allan, Channel 4’s former chief operating officer, who was in the running for the top job, also stepped down this year.

A Channel 4 spokesman said: “As we have shared publicly, under the leadership of our new CEO, we have been assessing Channel 4’s strategic direction, including a comprehensive review of the structure, shape and size of our organisation.

“We have committed to keeping Channel 4 staff updated in a timely and transparent way, so any organisational change will be shared with them first, and we won’t be commenting on speculation.”

data.title: Britain spends £84bn on energy imports
data.description:
The UK spent £84bn on buying oil, gas and electricity from abroad last year, amid warnings that high taxes are killing jobs in the North Sea and risking energy security.

The figure is the highest since 2022, when Vladimir Putin’s invasion of Ukraine plunged Europe into the most severe energy crisis in decades.

A report by Offshore Energies UK (OEUK), which represents the oil, gas, hydrogen, carbon capture and offshore wind industries, also said imports accounted for more than 40pc of the country’s energy needs. It warned that this leaves families and firms more vulnerable to global disruption.

Energy prices have come under immense pressure from Donald Trump’s war with Iran. Last week, Labour delayed a decision on whether to approve the Jackdaw gas field and Rosebank oil project in the North Sea, which its backers say will boost energy security.

Gas prices in the UK have in recent days spiked to a four-year high, while oil prices surged as high as $108.50 a barrel.

The report warned that successive governments have undermined the UK’s domestic oil and gas sector, accelerating a decline in domestic production.

The UK will need 561 billion cubic metres (bcm) of gas in the decade to 2035, it noted. The UK is expected to produce only 176bcm over this period. However, OEUK said this figure could be as high as 288bcm if the Government adopted “an investable fiscal regime and a pragmatic approach to licencing”.

If it does not, liquefied natural gas (LNG) imports could make up 46pc of supply by 2035, as opposed to only 6pc in a scenario where domestic production is prioritised.

The report warned: “LNG should be treated as a complement to domestic production, not a substitute. Future Norwegian piped imports also cannot be taken for granted.”

Norwegian officials have warned that supplies from the North Sea are in decline, threatening supplies to Britain, which relies on the Scandinavian country for around half of its gas.

LNG imports from the US rose by more than a third last year, increasing “exposure to global market volatility, geopolitical risk and higher lifecycle emissions”, the report said.

Three quarters of the LNG bought by the UK comes from the US, according to separate government figures.

The UK’s industrial energy consumption has meanwhile slumped to more than a 50-year low, amid industrial decline and greater power efficiency.

Enrique Cornejo, from OEUK, said: “It is concerning that we are importing more LNG, when we could produce half of our demand of gas for the coming years domestically with domestic resources. From the perspective of climate and emissions as well, LNG imports are more than three times more carbon-intensive compared to the average footprint of emissions in domestic [production]”.

The trade body urged Andy Burnham to scrap the Energy Profits Levy next year rather than in 2030, when the Government is planning to replace it with a 35pc tax on oil and gas sales.

Bringing in the oil and gas revenue levy three years early would help boost receipts by £14.9bn over the next decade, OEUK estimates.

The levy would have a less damaging effect on driving away investment, with £12.6bn of the boost to receipts coming from additional payroll taxes.

The report said: “The existing energy profits levy was introduced in response to a short-term price shock that has since ceased. The levy no longer reflects the market conditions and is constraining long-term investment in the UK continental shelf.”

data.title: CrossCountry cancels almost all trains after power cut
data.description:
CrossCountry has cancelled almost all its trains after a power cut at its Birmingham headquarters.

The long-distance rail operator warned of “significant disruption” on Sunday and said that services “across almost all routes will be withdrawn until further notice”.

The Birmingham city centre power cut has disrupted operations at CrossCountry’s main control centre, meaning systems used to manage its trains are unavailable.

The only CrossCountry route still running is between Peterborough and Stansted airport, calling at March, Ely and Cambridge.

CrossCountry tickets are being accepted via any reasonable route on all other train companies’ services, according to National Rail Enquiries. A normal service is expected to run on Monday.

A spokesman for CrossCountry said: “A power cut in Birmingham city centre has affected the building where our control centre is located. As a result, many of the systems our control teams use to manage the railway are currently unavailable.

“Although colleagues are working hard to safely operate services using alternative processes, CrossCountry services will be significantly disrupted on Sunday Aug 23.

“While we will run as many trains as possible, passengers should expect significant reductions to services and cancellations across almost all routes throughout the day. We are sorry to passengers affected by this significant and unforeseen disruption.

The National Grid operates the electricity distribution network serving Birmingham city centre.

On Aug 7, a similar power cut in Manchester caused a power cut at a Network Rail signalling control centre, leading to chaos across the north-west of England as all trains came to a standstill as a safety precaution.

The incident was triggered by a fault at a transformer in Ardwick, which provides energy for Network Rail’s Manchester Rail Operating Centre.

Heidi Alexander, the Transport Secretary, said: “I am concerned to hear about a power outage affecting CrossCountry rail services, which I know will be very frustrating to passengers.

“I’ve asked publicly owned operators to lay on extra services where possible. We’ve also sent Network Rail power teams who are on-site and working to restore power and systems as soon as possible.”

A National Grid electricity distribution spokesman said on Sunday afternoon: “Our engineers are on site working to repair a fault affecting CrossCountry’s Birmingham control centre.

“We’re working closely with CrossCountry to restore power safely as soon as possible. We understand the frustration caused by disrupted journeys and are sorry for the inconvenience to passengers.”

Travellers delayed by more than half an hour are eligible to claim Delay Repay compensation from the train company via its website.

data.title: Ryanair boss apologises over ‘rapists’ comments
data.description:
Michael O’Leary, the Ryanair boss, has issued a belated apology for comparing rival airlines to “rapists”.

The outspoken chief executive released a video message on Friday afternoon to apologise for the “considerable upset and offence” his comments caused.

It marks a considerable climbdown for Mr O’Leary after he initially refused to apologise last week.

The row erupted after the Irish airline boss recently said that some travellers were “desperate to get to Ryanair’s low fares because they can’t afford to fly with the high-fare rapists around Europe”.

His comments prompted a call from Rachel Morrogh, the head of the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre, for a “swift apology to survivors of rape and sexual violence”.

She said that Ireland’s National Rape Crisis Helpline had received an uptick in the number of calls from rape victims left “upset and distressed” by Mr O’Leary’s “lazy” comments.

Mr O’Leary initially defended his comments but has since rowed back.

In a video message posted online, Mr O’Leary said he apologised “sincerely and unreservedly”, especially to victims of sexual violence and rape.

He told Virgin Media News on Friday: “Last week, at a press conference in Dublin, I used the term ‘rapists’ to describe the high fares of our competitor airlines. I was quizzed by the press if I was trivialising rape.

“I will try to learn from this mistake and do better in the future. Thank you.”

His apology struck a significantly different tone to his earlier rebuttal to Ms Morrogh: “I was asked what I thought of rape and answered that it was a heinous crime.

“I was also asked if describing high-fare competitor airlines as ‘high-fare rapists’ somehow trivialised the crime of rape, and I was clear in my view that it did not.

“You are entirely free to hold a different opinion. But since I clearly did not trivialise the heinous crime of rape, I will certainly not be issuing any apology.”

It is not Mr O’Leary’s first brush with controversy.

He was criticised in 2020 for reportedly claiming that the largest terror threat to airlines “will generally be males of a Muslim persuasion”.

The Muslim Council of Britain said Mr O’Leary’s comments were “racist and discriminatory”.

Ryanair subsequently denied that Mr O’Leary was seeking to profile Muslim men and said he was instead “calling for more effective airport security checks”.

However, the airline did apologise for any offence caused by what it described as an inaccurate headline.

Ryanair was contacted for comment.

data.title: Sewage dumped into rivers as rain overwhelms water system
data.description:
Water companies are pumping sewage into rivers as ageing wastewater systems struggle to cope with the return of rain.

Campaign group River Action said there had been 4,600 sewage spill incidents across England and Scotland in the past 48 hours as storm overflows were overwhelmed.

Sewage has been flowing into the River Derwent in Derbyshire for 15 hours, while a spill into the River Windrush in Oxfordshire has been ongoing for 13 hours.

In the UK, a sewage spill is considered legal if it happens during exceptionally heavy rain and only if the sewage is discharged through an outlet named in the water company’s permit.

The incidents in recent days follow the return of rain after weeks of drought, with thunderstorms forecast across England during the bank holiday weekend.

However, Feargal Sharkey, the musician-turned-rivers campaigner, said the level of sewage seeping into the country’s rivers reflected the poor state of Britain’s water system rather than the weather.

Mr Sharkey said: “When there’s the merest hint of rain, copious amounts of sewage are dumped into our rivers and into the water around our beaches. Yet again the profiteering and failure of our water companies to invest is exposed.”

Thames Water spilt effluent into rivers for more than 100,000 hours in 2025, despite it being a dry year.

Severn Trent Water was the only water company to receive a top rating for its environmental performance last year, but nonetheless recorded more than 30,000 spillage incidents.

Utility companies are in the middle of an investment programme meant to reduce sewage spills. Water UK, which represents Britain’s water companies, said the industry was “tripling investment over the next five years to halve spills from storm overflows and upgrade the capacity of 1,700 wastewater treatment works”.

However, Mark Lloyd, the chief executive of River Action UK, said the investment was too little, too late.

“It is disgraceful that funding for new infrastructure to prevent sewage overflows – and for maintenance of existing assets – was restricted over the past 20 years,” he said.

Mr Lloyd added that the recent spillages were particularly bad, as the preceding drought meant the sewage was potentially more environmentally damaging.

He told The Telegraph: “Sewage overflows after long dry periods can be particularly damaging because there can be accumulations of concentrated sewage in the network that get flushed out into rivers that have low flows and oxygen levels, greatly increasing the impact on fish, invertebrates and other wildlife.”

Andy Burnham has pledged to assert greater control of water companies, saying this month that he was “angry” about the industry’s performance, including on pollution.

data.title: Boots in £7.5bn sale talks with billionaire family behind Primark
data.description:
Boots is in talks to sell itself for £7.5bn to the family behind Primark and an Australian pharmacy chain.

The billionaire Weston family, which owns Primark, is weighing up a bid that would see the chemist scrap plans for a London listing, according to the Financial Times.

The retail giant is understood to be in talks alongside Sigma Healthcare, an Australian pharmacy group, about a possible takeover of the 177-year-old chemist from Sycamore Partners, its private equity owner.

A takeover of Boots would derail plans for a stock market listing. The recent appointment of Alex Baldock – the former Currys boss credited with turning around the electronics retailer – as chief executive had fuelled speculation that Boots was being prepared to join the London Stock Market. 

Insiders had previously suggested that a flotation valuing the chain at up to £7bn was “always the plan”.

News of the talks came as Boots revealed that profits jumped by a quarter to £337m last year, as demand for weight-loss jabs, vaccinations and beauty products helped drive sales growth.

The Westons are one of the world’s richest retail families. Through their sprawling business empire they already control Primark-owner Associated British Foods (ABF), as well as Fortnum & Mason and major supermarket and pharmacy chains in Canada.

A deal would also deepen the family’s ties to British retail just months after it unveiled plans to split Primark from ABF, ending a six-decade partnership between the fashion chain and the conglomerate’s food operations.

Sigma, meanwhile, is a fast-growing Australian healthcare group best known for its links to Chemist Warehouse, Australia’s largest pharmacy retailer.

It has recently signalled ambitions to expand internationally and only last month entered the UK market through a pharmacy joint venture in and around London.

Hundreds of stores closed

A sale of Boots has been talked about for years. Walgreens first tried to offload it in 2022, before abandoning the effort when bids failed to meet expectations.

Sycamore Partners revived expectations of a breakup when it bought Walgreens Boots Alliance last year and carved out Boots as a standalone unit.

Boots has spent the past two years trying to improve its attractiveness to potential bidders. 

It has closed hundreds of under-performing UK stores as part of a broader cost-cutting drive, including a programme to shut branches, trimming its footprint from about 2,200 stores to roughly 1,900 in 2024.

At the same time, the chain has benefited from a boom in private healthcare services and a push into premium beauty brands, with online sales also rising sharply as more shoppers turned to its app and delivery partnerships.

The Weston family already has a presence in the pharmacy sector through Shoppers Drug Mart, a Canadian chain with more than 1,300 locations that it acquired in a multibillion-pound deal more than a decade ago.

Boots declined to comment.

data.title: Mike Ashley’s Harvey Nichols takeover ‘ethically dubious’
data.description:
Mike Ashley’s takeover of Harvey Nichols was “ethically dubious”, the boss of a UK fashion house has suggested.

Ewan Venters, the executive chairman of Paul Smith, criticised Mr Ashley’s purchase of the struggling department store last month using a controversial so-called pre-pack administration, which has left its suppliers facing substantial losses.

He said: “I personally find this whole thing about pre-pack administrations just dubious in terms of ethics and the way business gets done.

“I think it’s about £300m due to a whole bunch of suppliers and people. The latest talk is that 15p in the pound is what they might recover. I find it all a bit odd and I don’t think that’s a kind way of doing business.”

“On the other hand, maybe Harvey Nichols was about to go to the wall and maybe Mike and his team will hold that brand and keep it going. But let’s see.”

Mr Venters said that he hoped the Harvey Nichols brand survives because the high street needs it.

Harvey Nichols fell into administration on Aug 13 owing £270.5m to its creditors.

It was immediately acquired on the same day by Mr Ashley’s Frasers Group, the British retail group that also owns Sports Direct and House of Fraser, in a deal that used a fast-track insolvency process that will leave the department chain’s creditors facing unpaid debts.

Under the terms of the takeover, early-stage estimates from administrators FTI Consulting show the department store’s creditors will receive no more than 15pc of what they are owed.

Brands including Victoria Beckham, Canada Goose and Jimmy Choo are each owed hundreds of thousands of pounds.

Frasers Group reportedly paid around £40m to acquire Harvey Nichols’ six stores as well as its online and international franchise businesses.

The company, which has taken on more than 1,000 Harvey Nichols employees, has said there will be significant restructuring.

Michael Murray, the group’s chief executive, has said “meaningful change” is needed at Harvey Nichols and this will require “tough choices”.

Mr Ashley told the FT in August that Harvey Nichols was in a “death spiral” and it would be a “huge challenge” to turn the chain around.

The retail tycoon has a long history of hoovering up struggling rivals at big discounts.

Frasers Group’s past acquisitions using pre-pack administrations include bike retailer Evans Cycles and clothing brand Jack Wills.

Mr Venters was formerly the boss of luxury food retailer Fortnum & Mason and then head of global contemporary art gallery Hauser & Wirth.

He was appointed to the board of Paul Smith in February 2025 to review a business that had reported losses for six years in a row. He was made executive chair last October.

Mr Venters also told the BBC that working from home “just doesn’t work for young people” and urged the Government to stay out of decisions over where employees are based.

Louise Haigh, the First Secretary of State, told the Trades Union Congress (TUC) earlier this week that Labour will make it harder for employers to block people’s requests to work remotely.

Frasers Group was contacted for comment.
